speakerposition: Speaker of the House of Commons
maintopic: HOURS OF SITTING FOR BALANCE OF PRESENT SESSION
speechtext:
Our hours of sitting for the balance of the present session have been changed by some special orders, and it might be of assistance to hon. members if I were to recite the new sitting hours established by the special orders that have been adopted and those that have not been changed and still remain in effect according to present standing orders.
Pursuant to standing orders and to special orders made on March 27 and March 30 last, the hours of sitting of the house for the balance of the present session, unless otherwise provided at a later date, will be as follows: Monday, Tuesday and Thursday, 11 a.m. to 1 p.m., 2.30 p.m. to 6 p.m., 8 p.m. to 10 p.m.; Wednesday, 2.30 p.m. to 6 p.m., 8 p.m. to 10 p.m., Friday and Saturday, 11 a.m. to 1 p.m., 2.30 p.m. to 6 p.m. I thought this would help hon. members and others who are interested in our proceedings.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before motions are proceeded with I should like to raise a question of privilege. I do this because I understand that by the rules the speech which was made yesterday while I was not in the house is now in the position that I cannot reply to it because we have voted on the question which was then before the house.
Hence on a question of privilege I should like to point out that the hon. member for Moose Mountain (Mr. McCullough), when I was out meeting a delegation on potatoes yesterday, made some rather serious charges involving me personally and a livestock breeder in Alberta named P. J. Rock.
The first statement I wish to refer to was that P. J. Rock is "perhaps one of the greatest Liberal supporters in the province of Alberta." When I was first introduced to P. J. Rock- and it is now about 20 years ago, when I was attending the Royal at Toronto-a previous minister of agriculture in the province of Alberta introduced me after saying this: "This gentleman is one of the best livestock breeders in Canada but he is not a supporter of our party". As a result of that introduction I have never discussed politics with P. J. Rock. I have always confined myself to discussing livestock matters and ideas with him; and on each occasion that I have been with him I have been at the Toronto Royal or the Calgary Stampede, and there has always been a sufficient number of people about of all political parties so it was not a very good opportunity to discuss politics.
The other two occasions on which I have met Mr. Rock or have been with him are these. One occasion was when the livestock people asked me to speak at a livestock judging contest which was being held at Mr. Rock's farm about 20 years ago. I have forgotten the exact date, but it was shortly after I became minister. The only other time was in Calgary a year ago at a meeting at the exhibition grounds.
This further statement also comes from his speech made yesterday: Rumours persist that (a) some of these sheep have not been destroyed; (b) substitutions have been made; (c) some sheep were moved from P. J. Rock's flock to a farm in Manitoba. Then the hon. member said: "I am inclined to believe these rumours." Those are not charges against me. They are charges against Mr. Rock. I submit that it would have been more appropriate for him to have made those charges outside of this house rather than under the protection of this house.
The third statement to which I wish to refer is this: "It is now up to the minister to clear the air."
What I wish to suggest is this. I know I must have the unanimous consent of the house in order to have the suggestion agreed to, so with the unanimous consent of the house I suggest that the committee on agriculture and colonization be convened to meet tomorrow, Wednesday, April 3, at eleven o'clock; that the charges contained in the speech of the

subtopic: MILEAGE ALLOWANCES AND LIVING EXPENSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, yesterday the hon. member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt) asked a question of myself and of my colleague the Minister of Labour. The question was:
Are employees of the Department of National Revenue and the unemployment insurance commission paid mileage and living expenses when compelled to be absent from their respective offices on government business? If so, are these extra allowances considered as income for the purpose of taxation?
At that time I undertook to reply without notice, and I misunderstood the reference to allowances. Actually, travel regulations have been laid down by a series of orders in council which provide for the reimbursement of travel expenses incurred on government business by persons employed in the public service. The reimbursement of such expenses is not considered as income for the purpose of taxation.

Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Prime Minister. My question arises out of the statement read in the house by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources on March 26. The Prime Minister will recall it included a statement made by the Minister of Fisheries in connection with the International River Improvements Act, giving the federal government jurisdiction over works constructed on rivers crossing the international boundary and over the flow of water in those rivers crossing the border. The statement further indicated that the federal government would be prepared to assist in the construction of publicly-owned power sites in British Columbia, Nova Scotia and New Brunswick.
Will the government, on the basis of this statement, assist in the cost of development of the $40 million publicly-owned power site now being undertaken at Estevan in my constituency?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister):
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
maintopic: ESTEVAN, SASK.-INQUIRY AS TO FEDERAL ASSISTANCE POLICY

Mr. Speaker, I would not like my answer to imply that I agree with the construction the hon. gentleman places on the statement that is in writing on the records of this house, but I can say to him there has been no suggestion from the authorities of the province of Saskatchewan that they would wish any assistance from the federal government in connection with this Estevan project. But the policy, such as it really is, is available for consideration in connection with any project in any province that would fit the requirement of appearing to be an economical, self-liquidating project.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I direct a question to the Secretary of State for External Affairs. Now that there has been an opportunity for the advisory committee on the United Nations emergency force to confer with Mr. Ham-marskjold since his return from his interviews with Nasser in Cairo, can the minister bring the house up to date concerning the functions of that force at the present time?
I ask this particularly because of dispatches this morning from the United Nations in New York which indicate that Mr. Hammarskjold had stated that the United Nations emergency force is now to "assist"-with that word in quotation marks-the Egyptians in the Gaza strip policing. Also, two or three days ago there were dispatches to the effect that the members of the force were now to be considered as guests of Egypt.

speakeroldname: Hon. L. B. Pearson (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: EXTERNAL AFFAIRS
subsubtopic: STATEMENT RESPECTING POSITION OF UNITED NATIONS EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the United Nations emergency force is deployed inside the Gaza strip and along the Egyptian side only of the demarcation line. The headquarters of the force remains in Gaza city, and the base for the force is being removed from El Arish, a town in Egyptian territory, to the town of Rafa, which is inside the Gaza strip.
As a result of discussions in Cairo between the Secretary General of the United Nations and General Bums and the government of Egypt, requirements were laid down by General Burns as being necessary for the continued operation of the forces in the Gaza strip and to make its functioning on the demarcation line effective. Those requirements were agreed to by the government of Egypt in so far as the co-operation of that government was required and a statement on this matter was issued yesterday by the secretary general, to which my hon. friend has referred today. The first paragraph of that statement, which is the important one, reads as follows:
The advisory committee-
This statement is a message from the secretary general to the government of Egypt.
The advisory committee notes with appreciation the secretary general's statement on the understanding reached with the government of Egypt
Inquiries of the Ministry concerning the arrangements under which the United Nations emergency force would operate and which are established in accordance with the requirements of the force as presented by the commander. If, in practice, these arrangements were to prove insufficient or unsatisfactory the committee would revert to the issue and consider with the secretary general such further proposals as he might make or wish to make to the government of Egypt in order to provide for satisfactory conditions for the functioning of the force.
Mr. Speaker, it was the unanimous view of the advisory committee that the arrangements made between General Burns and Mr. Ham-marks j old and the authorities in Gaza and in Cairo should be satisfactory for the effective functioning of the force inside the Gaza strip and on the demarcation line.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while this budget debate has progressed in a rather chequered way, one day on and one day off, nevertheless we who have observed this house for some time are always satisfied-despite the variety of parties, the differences of opinions and the novel philosophies that are presented from time to time-that we have common and mutual desires and worthy objectives as to what is best for the country, its economic welfare, national security and so on.
On the other hand today I believe-and I think I can observe it-that the people of this country are keenly concerned. They are especially concerned with reference to major problems. They are concerned with reference to the state of agriculture. They are concerned about the tremendous adverse balances of trade and the disproportionate amount of that trade which has been with the commonwealth countries and European countries, about all our trading eggs being in one basket. As well they are concerned about high taxes. Many people are concerned greatly over the ever-increasing interest rates that affect so many persons.
The present budget, however, offers no solution whatever for any of these particular problems. In fact it is barren of any conception that there is in any of these problems any danger to our national economy. The government seem to be so quiet and smug that they cannot be alarmed about anything. It is
[Mr. MacEachen.l
certainly a pre-election document, intended to charm more than to alarm the people of Canada at this particular time.
I realize that there are some minor changes. However, these fundamental issues are quietly disregarded while election sops and hand-outs are more or less noisily paraded at this time. They boldly reduce taxes on pickles, prunes,, pies and mustard for the housewife, but they maintain higher costs than ever; I refer to the mortgage costs of the home owner. They bring in a reduction in the price of bubble gum but they keep the tax on the baby's boots. They do many little things in a small way.
I realize that there is some spirit of generosity in this pre-election budget, because I find that the aged have had their pensions increased sufficiently to buy two extra cups of coffee per day. Some of our children have had their pensions increased by at least a maximum of 4 cents a day. How far this will go for the purposes for which it was intended is hard to say. However, there is one thing that is certain. There never was so little spread so far so close to an election. The real issues concerning the people have been carefully disregarded. Nothing has been done to help solve any of these other problems. For five years this government has been complacent. It has been growing more complacent all the time, a fact which seems in keeping with the situation when a government gets old and tired and has been in office too long. But never before have I known them to so smugly disregard essentials and to play around with so many small issues which they believe will serve a temporary purpose. These other issues are the intelligent concern today of the farmers, the businessmen, the home owners and many others from coast to coast in this dominion.
Today the situation of agriculture in our so-called new society is alarming thousands and thousands of experienced farmers, and is confusing many young farmers throughout Canada as to whether they should carry on. I know the minister tells them all is well. The Minister of Trade and Commerce tells them everything is fine. So far as the government is concerned we have had no leadership in agriculture for the last 20 years. We have had "followership". The minister rises and tells us from time to time that he had a deputation of a few farmers down to see him and they told him what to do. Sometimes he follows their advice and sometimes he does not, but mostly he follows it.
However, I have not heard of any real, concrete assistance to help in any real way.

At times we are told to produce more. At other times we are told to produce less. People are somewhat confused. One year we are told that we have 78 million pounds of butter and that it is not too much of a surplus. The next year we are told that we have 38 million, and that it will be about a reasonable and adequate amount. Hence it is difficult for the farmers to know just which way to move.
I realize that there has been a great deal of controversy with reference to parity prices. Many farmers throughout the dominion feel, and I believe rightly so, that they have not had a proper share of our national income. When you stop to think of it, Mr. Speaker, you will find that in this dominion we have had a great many safeguards for other classes of people. Much of this legislation has been good. We have unemployment insurance, which costs the taxpayers of Canada $60 or $70 million. It has been an excellent thing for those men who have been out of employment. It would have been an excellent thing for those who had been out of employment on other occasions but who did not have it. I am extremely glad that we have it now.
We have minimum wage laws. I do not think there is an hon. member in this house who does not believe that this is sound legislation in keeping with the advancement of our modern society. We have fixed freight rates for the products the farmers haul on the railroads. We have fixed rates for almost every other form of public ownership. I think it is only reasonable that the farmer should feel that he is the forgotten man in this whole shuffle and change in our national society. We are not living in the days in which we were living some years ago. This is a new order, you might call it. It is not the same. The labourer is worthy of his hire. Labour is receiving much more of the national product; and so it goes all the way along the line. We have subsidies for mines which have been to advantage.
However, when the farmer asks for parity he is told by the government that it is not sound. Very little effort has been made to meet his complaints in that regard. I realize that some propositions have been put forward that we believe might be economically unsound. Nevertheless we have had no concrete effort put forward. The farmers of Canada are sorely disappointed. They are disgruntled at the present time; they are dissatisfied, and they are confused as to what is going to become of Canadian agriculture.
I am satisfied, Mr. Speaker, that we must grapple with this situation; that we must have a degree of parity prices that will
The Budget-Mr. Rowe give the farmer a square deal in this new form of what might be termed a subsidized economy.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Why did you
vote against our amendment, then?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Because it was like many other proposals you have made; it was unsound, and would not solve the problem. I have never been enamoured, confused or surprised by anything that might come from my hon. friend in that regard. I know his intentions are good, but his solutions are often spectacular and novelistic.
I do feel, Mr. Speaker, that we have a very dangerous situation in this country. There is no one who knows anything about agriculture who is not aware that we have had falling prices for the last four or five years. I have been closely associated with agriculture for some time and I can recall, as I think the Minister of Agriculture can, that even in the days when the dollar was worth more than it is today farmers were selling barley for 96 cents a bushel and wheat for $1.20 a bushel before world war I.
It is true that at times those products have sold for less since those early days. I can hear someone say what about the thirties? The Minister of Agriculture will not say that now, because history shows that those conditions resulted from the failure of those who now sit to your right to pay proper attention to the trend of the times.
We had our storage glutted with unsold wheat just as we have at the present time. We had practically lost every vestige of the British market. We have lost that market twice now under the guidance of this same group. They say three times and out, but I believe they will be out the second time. The Minister of Agriculture smiles in satisfaction, believing that they will never be defeated in his time. In all these years we have not had anything in the way of real leadership from the government in meeting this basic problem of the rise and fall in prices.
Then there is the problem of the mechanization of agriculture. When I entered this house we had about 40 per cent of the population engaged in agriculture, whereas today we have about 15 per cent. I know that some of this decrease in the number of people engaged in agriculture is attributable to mechanization, but some of it is attributable to the fact that young men see very little hope in a career in agriculture unless agriculture is given some form of assistance, co-operation, you might say, from the government.
I am not going to pursue that at any length because I know there are other problems that
2964	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Rowe are also very important. Everyone who wants to build a home is interested in the tight money policy of the government. They are trying to impose this tight money policy upon the people. Everybody who pays taxes is equally concerned about the loose money policy of the government. They have taken $400 million more from the people than they said they would take, and they have spent $200 million more than they thought they would spend. Yet they turn around and say, "We will increase the bank rate so the worker cannot build his home and the farmer cannot get a loan to produce more cattle or hogs". One will rise and tell you, almost with the chestiness of an economist, that production will solve inflation. Another will rise and tell you that we cannot lend any money to increase production. One will rise and tell you not to spend any more money, and another will rise and tell you he spent $200 million more than he thought he was going to spend. Mr. Speaker, stop and think what really has happened. No wonder these people are concerned. No wonder the heather is almost on Are.
My friends laugh. These smug, quiet old gentlemen have been in power so long they do not know what is happening. Some of us who have not had as much responsibility in this house as they have had, and who have listened to the rumblings in the mulberry bushes, have heard the farmer talking. We have heard the labour man talking and the businessman. I shall not name the ridings in which I heard these things because I do not want to make the ministers nervous. You hear people say, "I have voted Grit for the last time".
Why is that? It is because the Liberals have been in power so long they have become smug and complacent. They do not know what is happening. This government has raised interest rates six times in 14 months. Why was that done? Was it to stop production, to stop the spending of money? If a shortage of goods is going to increase inflation, then can the Minister of Finance tell me how fewer houses will make houses cheaper? Is it going to make it better for the home owners to increase the interest rates on mortgages? Is it going to make it better to have the governor of the Bank of Canada say that liquid assets must be raised to 15 per cent and that 7 per cent of them must be put in short-term loans? It must be done in a hurry or you are not going to produce much.
It is no wonder that our bank managers are somewhat concerned, as well as our farmers. Our farmers are concerned because they do not know when, if ever, money is


going to come. The bank manager is concerned because he does not know where in the world it is going, and they refuse to let him lend money. The Minister of Finance is concerned because he does not know what the governor of the Bank of Canada is going to say, and the governor of the Bank of Canada is worried because he does not know what the Minister of Finance is going to say. Everybody is worried, yet they have the business of this country by the scruff of the neck. Today no one can build even a garage without finding out what the Minister of Finance and the governor of the Bank of Canada say. It does not matter what credit you have at the bank. By some arrangement they have things tied up so tight there is only half as much money available for loans as there was last year, even if you have credit. In fact if you have,-I would not say the right connection, but if you approach them in a diplomatic way you can do better if you do not have any credit at the bank.
I am just as worried about inflation as anybody else in Canada. I am just as worried as the Minister of Finance is, but I am worried more about his novelistic cure-all than I am about the inflation itself. A farmer may go to a bank and want to borrow money to produce 10,000 pounds more beef. Even if he has the credit he is refused the loan. Is that going to stop inflation?
Make the houses scarce so that the builders will bid against each other; make the beefsteak scarcer so it will cost more. To my mind, Mr. Speaker, it is novel and unsound.
I would suggest to the Minister of Finance and to his governor of the Bank of Canada that they call in some others, some other smart men, some other bank managers, some men who have had as much experience and more than either of them, and sit down as a committee and try to iron out a policy that will elicit the confidence of the business people of this country, the confidence of people who are building houses, the confidence of people who are carrying on construction, the confidence of people who will eventually, if given encouragement, lower rather than increase the prices of houses, lower rather than increase the cost of other products by increased production.
I realize that the government has problems; in fact I realize it more than I imagine they do at any time, because they think as long as they are there there are no problems. In the last seven years they have increased the taxes of this country by 100 per cent. It seems to be the watchword of the Minister of Finance and of the government that if we want prosperity we must tax the people more; if we

want production we must increase the interest rates. It is no wonder it is a brand of economy that many of the leading lights in the financial world are growing concerned about, and especially some bank managers.
We have mentioned on this side of the house on many occasions-it has been brought to the attention of the government time and time again-that we have an adverse balance of trade that threatens the economic independence of this country; that it is growing by leaps and bounds. It is growing steadily every month, but even that does not shake them. They will not listen to the boards of trade, the chambers of commerce, the manufacturers' associations, the farmers, the professors in universities and many people who have given some thought to these problems and who are intelligently concerned about where we are going.
I can well recall, Mr. Speaker, when we had an adverse balance of trade with the United States alone of $300 million in a year. That alarmed those in power at that time. It is $1,400 million now, but that does not even get a serious look from them. In fact the Minister of Trade and Commerce says it is the healthiest thing that has happened in Canada; it is a sign of good economic health, a sign of our abounding prosperity.
It is true that the United States likes this country and we like them. It is true that their investments are a great boon to our prosperity. I know my hon. friends across the way would like to say that this party has been opposed to their investments. Why, Mr. Speaker, it was this party and the policy of this party 75 years ago that started the real investment by the United States of America in Canada, by a sound fiscal policy. But we have never felt, and many more have never felt, that you could continue year after year to buy more and more than you sell and be prosperous, even though your customer is satisfied to lend you $500 million a year to pay for it.
What we bought last year I believe was an all-time high, and we had an adverse balance of trade of $1,298 million on commodity trade alone, or about $1,600 million of an adverse balance on current account. When you get up there, Mr. Speaker, $100 million does not make much difference. A country the size of ours might go broke on an adverse balance of $1,300 million almost as quickly as it might go broke on $1,400 million. It is like the Irishman who said he would rather go broke on $100,000 than $10,000 if he was going to go broke.
The Minister of Finance says it is a better sign of prosperity to have $1 billion against you than to have $500 million. I beg your pardon; the Minister of Finance has never
The Budget-Mr. Rowe been that reckless yet. It was the Minister of Trade and Commerce. I hope they get more cabinet solidarity before the election. I am not going to put the Minister of Finance on the spot.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You could not.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Because with these high taxes and high interest rates he has enough to worry about, without having the highest adverse balance of trade that we have ever had in our history. But, Mr. Speaker, that did not disturb them last year, and it did not disturb them in January and February of this year that we had a much higher adverse balance of trade in those two months than we had in the first two months of last year. It is up higher than ever before.
There are many people in this country, Mr. Speaker, who are beginning to wonder if it is a safe line of trade policy to buy, as we have, $4,400 million more in the last five years from the United States than we sold to them, even if they are good enough to agree that it is a nice policy and they are good enough to lend us the money to buy the goods. Perhaps this is such a fabulous country that we can stand it. It must be fabulously wealthy and resourceful to stand the management it has had in recent years.
I have had a little experience, Mr. Speaker, and I have watched parties in this parliament; I have watched business people try to make ends meet. I have had some problems in that regard myself on different occasions. I never could find ways and means by which I could steadily buy more than I could sell even if my customer lent me the money to pay for it, or my seller lent me the money to buy it, and be in a sounder economic position.
However, I do believe there is another danger which our people are worried about, bad and all as our adverse balance of trade is, and that is putting all our trade eggs in one basket. We have done that to a greater extent than any other nation in the world has ever done. Today we are trading with the United States of America to a greater extent than ever. It is true they are our friendly allies; it is true there is only an invisible border between us; it is true there are those in Canada who would like to join the United States and Canada. It is true there are those in Canada who would rather be closer to the United States than to the commonwealth. It is true it is a great country, the strongest industrial country in the world, the greatest and strongest ally of the free world. But, Mr. Speaker, is it sound for Canada, even if we are taking advantage of our friendship with the United States, to tie our kite entirely to them?
2966	HOUSE OF COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Rowe If prosperity fades there it is bound to fade here; if depression comes there it will come worse here. I do not think it is any sounder, Mr. Speaker, to put all our economic eggs in that basket alone, even though most of them will be there, than it is to listen to the United States of America on international and external affairs. One is just about as unsound as the other.
The only difference is that in economic affairs the United States has always seemed to know where it is going. In external affairs it does not seem to know where it has been or where it is going next. No matter where they lead this government follows them. When they disagree with Britain this government follows them. When they tell Britain to get out the government follows them. When they move in the government is ready to follow them.
In the matter of trade the same old argument is used. Yes, Mr. Speaker, I have heard in this house from these same apostles of free trade with the United States the same old argument used by the late leader of their party, "We must not provoke the United States of America." We could raise tariffs-countervailing tariffs, if you will- and we could raise duties, but we must not provoke them. We do not want to provoke the United States but there are one billion four hundred million reasons why we should take a look at what they are doing to us.
Mr. Speaker, I know the United States likes our country. I know it is a natural sequence to their policies and practices to have them invest to the extent they have in Canada. Today the United States has invested $13 billion-$13,000 million-in Canada. They have increased their investment by approximately $10 billion since the war. It is a fact, Mr. Speaker, as you and every hon. member within sound of my voice know, that a great deal of the money that is coming in here is for bonds and loans so we can pay for the adverse balance of trade.
Mr. Speaker, this government-I should say this party, for that is all it will be after the election-must take a look at the course we are following with regard to export and import trade. No matter what party is elected on June 10-and I should not make the announcement, because it is not my prerogative-this country must stop, look and listen as to where we are going in export and import trade. The condition must be equalized whether it is done by way of exchange or otherwise.
I am amazed that the Minister of Trade and Commerce would stand up in this house and tell us that an adverse balance in trade is a healthy sign, and leave the impression

that the more adverse our balance of trade is the healthier is our position, and then go to Minneapolis, Chicago or other places in the United States and tell them it cannot continue if we are to have economic soundness in Canada. That is not blowing hot and cold in the same country; it is only blowing hot in one country and cold in the other.
Mr. Speaker, there is another aspect of this which far transcends sentiment. It is hard, cold and rugged business sense from the standpoint of our economic soundness and international security. I am referring to the need for a different concept from what this government has toward our commonwealth relations. It is not good enough for the Minister of National Health and Welfare or the Prime Minister to chide us who say we should have closer commonwealth relations and say, "We love the motherland, the commonwealth, so much". It is interesting how they emphasize that. Why, they love her so much they do not think it is necessary to talk to her.

speechtext: Have you stopped?

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
We in this party have pleaded for commonwealth conferences. The Prime Minister says it is not necessary that we hold them. We are glad that at least the prime ministers are going to meet, but such a meeting is a far cry from a British commonwealth trade conference. The honeyed words of the Prime Minister and members of the government are fine, but just compare the government's attitude toward trade relationships with the commonwealth with that of Mr. Menzies of Australia. Stop and think of it. It is not a case as some suggest of Canada being tied to the apron strings of the United Kingdom, or as some would say, old Britain. That is not the point.
Just as agriculture today is in a new concept of Canadian society, as I have mentioned, the commonwealth is in a new concept of a society of new nations. It is no longer the old British empire or the old commonwealth we talk about; it is now a society of more or less new and independent nations, but it is based on the friendships and the traditions and the soundest relationship that any group of nations ever had in the world's history. That relationship is interlocked not only in trade matters but in matters of security.

Mr. Speaker, I realize the problem that exists today. I realize that we have a great market in the United States for many of our raw products; but I also realize, and you must too, that that country produces pretty much the same products we produce. If not, why do not these great champion salesmen the Minister of Trade and Commerce and the Minister of Agriculture sell the United States some of our surplus wheat and other surplus agricultural products?
You can tell me there are 10 billion reasons why they have that large surplus. The people of the United States are friends of ours. They speak the same language and produce the same products, but we have never in our history sold the United States as much mixed farm products in one year as we sold to Britain before the Liberal party came into power in 1921, and every dollar of that market was lost before they went out of power in 1930. We regained a great portion of it through British commonwealth conferences and the Liberal government has lost it again.
As Job said, "How long, O Lord, how long." How long can the people of Canada tolerate such a trade policy? That is what is wrong with our agricultural position. I believe through commonwealth trade conferences we could sit down and work out a sound economic commonwealth agreement.
Not only is this possible, but there never was a time when it was more important than now when western Europe is planning a free trade bloc. It is important that we examine our commonwealth relations, whether or not Britain becomes a member of that bloc. We should stop and think of the possibilities provided by close associations. The countries of western Europe have too many people and we have not enough people. Many of their people would be glad to settle here. There is ample opportunity here for many more people.
I believe it is equally important from the standpoint of international security that we examine our trade relationships, because the United Nations is shoved here and there, sometimes by Nasser and sometimes by Khrushchev, people without much similarity of background, traditions and other allegiances. And great as they may be and necessary as we may think they are, there is no secure basis for the united nations of the world other than a closely knit and firm understanding existing among the new society of free independent nations of the commonwealth, for that is what the old commonwealth is becoming. A close association between the countries of western Europe and the newly evolved commonwealth to my mind would mean a great deal. There has never
The Budget-Mr. Brisson been a time, Mr. Speaker, when it was more necessary to have conferences than now. There has never been a time when a government has talked so much about its friendship with the commonwealth and done so little about it, so far as conferences are concerned.
The leader of this party has repeated this, before he became leader and since, and that is one of the reasons the people across this country are today swinging behind the new leader of the Conservative party; also because this government has sat so smugly and complacently and has done nothing on these fundamental issues. He has not been saying it for election purposes. He is not saying it to attract political support; he is saying it from conviction. He has said it for five years in this parliament and on this side of the house.
The government has not, in my opinion, exploited its advantages so far as trade is concerned. I do not think our friendship is so great that we can be smug or that we do not need to talk about these matters; they concern us so much. I do think however, Mr. Speaker, that western Europe and the British commonwealth are important.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think it can be said that of all Canadian constituencies, mine is the one which, since 1950, has expanded more than any other. To convince the hon. representatives of the Canadian nation, sitting in this house, of the truth of such a statement, I need only mention the gigantic developments of the Iron Ore Company in the area of Seven Islands and Knob Lake, the undertakings of the Quebec Iron and Titanium at Havre St. Pierre, those of the Quebec Hydro on the Bersimis river, those of the Mid-Canada Line in the heart of Ungava, those of the British Aluminum Company at Baie Comeau, those of the Spar Mica at Baie Johan Beetz and those of Aconic Mining at Natashquan.
As a result of these investments of the order of one billion dollars, the industrial production of my riding has now reached almost $200 million. New towns, such as Shefferville and Hauterive, which now have a population of about 3,000 each, have been created. The town of Seven Islands now has a population of 8,000 as compared to 1,200 in 1950. At present, the total population of the constituency of Saguenay exceeds 56,000, double that of ten years ago.

The Budget-Mr. Brisson
It is by no means exaggerated, moreover, to state that during the same period lumbering, power development and mining have provided employment to a large number of outside workers, encouraged and stimulated the economic activity of the south shore of the St. Lawrence, not to mention that of the whole national economy. I might repeat at this point, by the way, what was stated by the chairman of the St. Lawrence Seaway Authority, the hon. Lionel Chevrier, according to whom the presence of iron ore in the Ungava had been the decisive argument which had promoted the Canadian government to proceed with the opening of the St. Lawrence seaway.
The economic prospects of the constituency of Saguenay seems even more impressive if we take into account its hydroelectric power potential which is of the order of 12 million h.p., its timber reserves which represent close to one fifth of the total forest area of the province of Quebec, the wealth of its mineral resources which have only just begun to be surveyed, the possibilities for further expansion of the industries already operating there and finally the projects of the Cartier Mining Company at Shelter Bay, those of the Canadian Javelin Company at Wabush Lake, those of the Fenimore Company at Ungava Bay, the harnessing of the Hamilton falls by the Brinco Company and the possible extension of the present Seven Islands-Knob Lake railway to Ungava Bay by the Quebec North Shore and Labrador Railway Company.
It will therefore be readily understood that the constituency of Saguenay will increase its production and its population fourfold and even fivefold over the next twenty-five years.
Following that statement, I should like to quote a few figures which were submitted to the Gordon commission by the board of trade of Baie Comeau.
In 1957, the production of pulpwood in my constituency will amount to one million cords valued at 25 million dollars; in 1958, it will reach 1,200,000 cords valued at 30 million dollars, and for the year 1981 it is predicted that production will reach two million cords valued at 60 million dollars.
In 1957, production of paper pulp will amount to 110,000 tons valued at 9 million dollars. In 1958, it will reach 125,000 tons valued at 10 million dollars and, for the year 1981, it is estimated that production will reach 250,000 tons valued at 25 million dollars.
The production of paper in 1957 will be
165,000	tons, valued at 21 million dollars; in 1958, it will be 180,000 tons, valued at

23 million dollars and, according to estimates for the year 1981, production will reach
300,000	tons worth 40 million dollars.
As regards iron ore, production in 1957 will amount to 13 million tons, valued at 143 million dollars. In 1958 it will be 2d million tons, valued at 220 million dollars and, in 1981, production will reach 35 million tons valued at 525 million dollars.
In 1958, production of aluminum will amount to 40,000 tons worth 20 million dollars; in 1981, it will be 300,000 tons valued at 180 million dollars.
In 1957, the production of electricity will represent 25,000 horsepower representing a value of 500 million dollars; in 1958, it will reach one million horsepower valued at 20 million dollars and, in 1981, three million horsepower valued at 60 million dollars.
We thus come to a total of $198,500,000 for the production of 1957, $323 million for 1958 and $890 million for 1981. If we add to this a steel plant at Seven Islands in 1981, when we can anticipate an annual production of $200 million, the annual production of Saguenay riding, in 1981, will have reached one billion 90 million dollars. If this figure is compared with the forecasts of the Gordon commission as to Canada's total production in 1981 ($75 billion), we see that Saguenay county alone will account, in 1981, for l/75th of our total national production.
On the basis of those figures, it should fittingly be stated in this house that the present Liberal government has closely co-operated with capital and labour to the unbelievable expansion of my riding. Since 1949, wharves and airports have multiplied and mail delivery has greatly improved. Employment has been more effectively managed by two employment offices.
Bush workers have benefited from unemployment insurance and fishermen will soon do so. For its part, the federal department of National Health and Welfare has distributed health and social security benefits. Moreover, the Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has enabled many of my electors to become home owners.
While cordially thanking the various ministers for giving my numerous requests favourable consideration on a great many occasions, I must remind them that my constituents will be expecting more of them over the next few years because I know that the Liberal party will once more obtain an expression of the elector's confidence come voting day.

With a normal population of 60,000 people and a floating population of an additional
50,000	during the winter, the Saguenay cannot get through the four winter months unless it can get at reasonable prices the various commodities it needs. On the other hand the shipping of the raw materials produced in my constituency cannot be interrupted for so long a time.
I hope that the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler), following the representations made to him by the hon. member for Rimouski (Mr. Legare) and myself, will not wait too long before providing the south shore of the St. Lawrence with a winter port, because winter ports are not lacking on the north shore. This would make trade between the north and the south shores of the St. Lawrence far easier. As a matter of fact, he would merely have to put an icebreaker in service to keep the river clear of ice all year round.
Now, Mr. Speaker, I must say that I would have liked the house to have an opportunity to discuss the resolution which I had put on the order paper on January the 8th last and according to the terms of which the Canadian National Railways would have been asked by the government to look into the possibility of building a railway line in the Saguenay district between La Malbaie and Seven Islands. May I be allowed, at least, to suggest that the study of this project be made during the next parliament since, in my view, it is essential that the people of the constituency of Saguenay be provided with means of transportation 365 days a year, for freight as well as for passengers.
If we expect the constituency of Saguenay to develop at the expected rate, it is indispensable that the industries already there have advantages similar to those enjoyed by other industries in other parts of this country. The various communities in my constituency need a year round service in order to be able to communicate between themselves.
There are two main problems which I wanted to bring to the attention of the house concerning the future of my constituency. I hope that the Liberal government may bring these projects about in the near future. They are both extremely important to the economy of Canada as a whole.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, as my colleagues who have preceded me have made clear, we of the C.C.F. have no confidence in the government which has brought down the budget now before the house. In our view there are at least two things that budget proposals ought
The Budget-Mr. Knowles to do. They should lay before the house fiscal measures designed to gear our economy to meet the nation's needs and to deal with the economic problems facing us at any given time. In the second place, budget proposals should make adjustments in taxation so as to remove unjust tax burdens from those unable to bear them and impose taxation on those who can afford to pay.
This budget does neither of these things. Therefore we regard it, as my colleague the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Cameron) has already pointed out, as a budget that is politically inept and economically unsound. Because the budget failed to grapple with the problems which are the proper subject matter of a budget we were not surprised that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) went out of bounds and chose in the course of his budget speech to talk about matters which he did not lay before the house in the form of resolutions or notices of motion. I refer to what he had to say regarding the changes that are proposed to be made in seven other statutes, statutes that come under the direction of the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin) or the Minister of Veterans Affairs (Mr. Lapointe.)
I think we are all quite clear on this point. The proposed changes in the various pension payments and in veterans benefits are outside the scope of budgetary proposals. They are not before us in the resolutions that will be considered by committee of the whole if the motion we are now debating is carried at a quarter to ten tonight. Nevertheless, because the minister realized the shortcomings of his budget as a budget he tried to cover up those shortcomings by taking unto himself the prerogative of announcing certain changes the government intends to make in seven other statutes now on our statute books. Those seven statutes are the Old Age Security Act, the Old Age Assistance Act, the Family Allowances Act, the Blind Persons Act, the Disabled Persons Act, the Pension Act and the War Veterans Allowance Act.
May I say that we welcome the fact that increases-I will bring in the adjectives later -are to be made in the allowances, benefits and pensions that are paid under the seven statutes to which I have referred. But I want to register very strongly our objection to the course the government has proposed for dealing with these very important statutes. I say to you, Mr. Speaker, on behalf of this group that the whole field of social security and the whole field of what we do for our

The Budget-Mr. Knowles veterans are too important to be dealt with in some makeshift way just on the eve of an election.
These matters call for full and proper consideration of the kind that we have been pleading for since this parliament met following the election in 1953. Everyone knows that the best arrangement that was ever made in the field of social security came as a result of long and hard study given to that matter by a special committee of parliament in 1950. Everyone knows that the best consideration of the welfare of our veterans has come out of committee deliberations by a committee composed of veterans representing all parties in this house.
We greatly regret that the government has seen fit, during the years of this parliament, to do nothing about these matters in the proper way and yet to come along, just on the eve of an election, with some makeshift device-which has not yet reached the floor of the house-to make miserable, miserly increases in the hope that they might have some influence on the electorate on June 10 or whatever the election date may be. We insist that increases there must be. The minister knows that he will have our support in making sure that those increases are brought into effect before this session ends, whenever it ends. But he also knows that he has our condemnation and that of all people who are interested in social security being dealt with on a proper basis for the way in which matters are being handled.
I also want to say something about the amount of the increases which the government has proposed. There are those who may argue that, in the case of the increases under the Pension Act,-the $125 rate that goes up to $150 and the $170 rate that goes up to $200, the one single, the other married-at least those increases are better than the others. But even those increases fall far short of what the Canadian Legion has requested; and it has been our experience across the years that the Legion is quite responsible in the requests that it makes to the government and to parliament. Apart from those increases to which some hon. members of the house like to refer more than to some of the others, may I say that the other increases are an insult to the good name of Canada and an insult to the pensioners and to the recipients who are covered by these various pieces of legislation.
Of course the amount which is best known to us is this $6 figure which was picked out of somebody's hat as an increase in the amount of the payment under the Old Age Security Act, the payment under the old Age Assistance Act, the payment under the Blind Persons Act and the payment under the

Disabled Persons Act. The $40 rate of pensions for people in those categories was arrived at in 1949. I know that the government likes to point out that universal old age pensions began in 1952. The Minister of National Health and Welfare in a speech on March 22 of this year referred to the fact that these other items of legislation came into being in 1952 or later. However, the fact is that $40 as a rate for old people and blind people-the other rates have been assimilated to these pensions-was arrived at in 1949; and any comparisons that are going to be made between what is paid after this session is over and the present figure must be comparisons between 1957 and 1949.
I remind hon. members that in 1949 the gross national product of this country was of the order of $16 billion a year. It is now of the order of $30 billion a year. That figure represents an increase of over 80 per cent. Yet the government asks our older people, our blind people and our disabled people to settle for an increase, in what we pay them out of our great wealth, of only 15 per cent or $6 a month. I say again that this $6 increase is an insult to those who are to receive it. But it is also an insult to the good name of Canada and an insult to the heart of the Canadian people which is essentially sound and wants to do the right thing by our older people, our blind, our disabled and all those who are the recipients of social security in one form or another.
At this point may I say a word with regard to the treatment accorded to one particular group. I refer to the single recipients under the War Veterans Allowance Act, be they veterans who are single or widows of veterans. We resent very deeply the way in which the government-though it has increased by some amount practically all of the other benefits, single or married-has refused to increase the $60 single rate which is paid under the War Veterans Allowance Act.
I know that the ceiling on permissible income has been increased. That is fine, in a sense, for those who are able to earn some other income. It is also a bit of a boon-a $4 boon-to recipients of the war veterans allowance who are over 70 years of age and are drawing old age security. I know also that it is possible for recipients of the war veterans allowance, by submitting themselves to a second means test, to apply for the assistance fund contribution and thereby to increase the total amount that they are receiving. But why should this particular group of people-the single veterans and the widows-under the War Veterans Allowance

Act be treated differently from other recipients of social security and veterans legislation and be put in the category of having to submit to a second means test or get extra money by a roundabout way? Why was it not possible to make an increase in their benefit rate as was done for all the other groups? We deplore most strongly the discriminatory attitude which the government has taken towards the single veteran and the widow under the War Veterans Allowance Act.
One of the answers of the government is that in certain respects it has reached the figures for which the Legion asked sometime ago. That answer does not correspond with the kind of messages we are now receiving from Legion branches. If the government wants to talk of what the Legion is asking for, I might point out that so far as the War Veterans Allowance Act is concerned the Legion has requested that the permissible income ceiling be raised to $1,200 single and $2,000 married. The government is still far short of meeting this very justifiable request.
I come back to the old age pension, the blindness allowance and perhaps one or two other social security benefits and I want to draw attention to what I regard as two of the most despicable tricks that any government has ever played. Out of his largesse, out of the magnanimity of his heart, the Minister of Finance stood up here on March 14 and announced an increase of $6 a month in old age security, old age assistance, the blindness allowance and the allowance for disabled persons, along with other increases.
My, he must have had to sharpen his pencils and work hard to find $6 per month out of our gross national product of $30 billion. But he did not tell us the whole story that night.
The rest of the story was told on March 22, eight days later, by the Minister of National Health and Welfare. We remember that particular speech. The Minister of National Health and Welfare had not given any indication he was going to speak in the budget debate but after my friend the hon. member for Winnipeg North (Mr. Stewart) recounted something of the interesting tour the minister had around the world, the minister found it possible to make a speech. In that speech he told us what the new ceilings would be with regard to the Old Age Assistance Act and the Blind Persons Act. I do not think he told us, at least I have not been able to find it anywhere, what the new ceilings would be under the Disabled Persons Act but I presume they will be similar to those under the Old Age Assistance Act.
The Budget-Mr. Knowles

The Minister of Finance has now told us two things. He has told us we will soon know what the ceilings are and he has told us that this matter will be dealt with by tabling supplementary estimates.
May I make my remarks on the basis of the new ceilings which the Minister of National Health and Welfare announced in his speech on Friday, March 22. He indicated that in the case of a single recipient of old age assistance the amount of the pension goes up by $6 and the amount of the permissible income goes up by $10. In one sense that is fine because it means that the single recipient of old age assistance will get the full $6 increase regardless of any other income he may have. But what did the Minister of National Health and Welfare tell us about the married couple on old age assistance? The Minister of Finance on March 14 gave such a couple $6 per month each, a total of $12. But the Minister of National Health and Welfare says the increase in the ceiling on permissible income for a married couple hoth of whom are on old age assistance will be from $1200 to $1320 per year, an. increase of $120 a year or $10 per month.
Let us carry that through, Mr. Speaker. Here is a married couple now drawing $80' per month under old age assistance because-both of them are between the ages of 65 and' 69. The ceiling on their income is $100 per month. They own their own home which is assessed as being worth $20 per month, so we will say they are at the ceiling of $100 per month. When the new rates come into-effect, will their pension go up from $80 to $92? No, the new ceiling is put at $110 per month so their pension will go up to only $90 per month. Every married couple where both the man and the wife are on old age assistance, in other words between 65 and 69, where they are presently at the ceiling so-far as the means test is concerned, will get an increase of only $10 per month instead of $12 per month. In other words, the Minister of Finance stood up on March 14 and said to married couples on old age assistance,
I am giving you $12 per month. The Minister of National Health and Welfare stood up eight days later and said, I am sorry but this government cannot afford it so we are taking back $2, $1 each. We are putting the married recipients of old age assistance in a special class, if they are at the means test ceiling. They will get, not this magnanimous $6 per month but only $5 per month. How small, how despicable, how mean, how low can a government get?

The Budget-Mr. Knowles
If it is bad, Mr. Speaker, for the government to act in this mariner with respect to two old people on old age assistance I ask you to consider the case of the blind. The government is doing the same thing with respect to the blind where there is a married couple both of whom are receiving the blindness allowance or one receiving the blindness allowance arid the other old age assistance. The Minister of National Health and Welfare made it clear in his speech on March 22 that in the case of a single recipient of blindness allowance the increase in the ceiling is greater than the increase in the allowance. So long as that is the case, each recipient gets the full increase. But in the case of the married couple, both of them blind and both on the blindness allowance, the ceiling is raised by $120 a year, from $1680 to $1800, which is $10 per month. So again, Mr. Speaker, you have this government putting $12 per month, $6 each, into the pockets of our blind people where they are married and both of them on the allowance, but if they are at the present means test ceiling then the government comes to those two blind people who cannot see them doing it, and takes back a dollar each. I say again, seldom has a government in this country stooped so low, seldom has a government in this country done anything so mean, so inhuman, so despicable-

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Stop being so melodramatic.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I thank my hon. friend for
his interjection'; that is all it is to him, melodrama. That is all it is to him, this inhuman action of this government. He regards it as something that should be praised and supported even when the facts are laid before him, even when the government, which I presume he still supports, pays a $6 increase but says to certain people, particularly blind people who are both on the allowance, "If you have a little bit that gets you up to the means test ceiling, we are sorry but we cannot afford to give $6 per month each; in your case, we will make it only $5 per month each." I say that anybody in this House of Commons who votes confidence in a government that stoops to a trick like that-well, at least he should have his head examined but before long he will have a chance to have his politics examined.
As if this sort of performance is not enough of an insult to our older people, our blind and our disabled, paying them so little in the first place and then putting in these tricks with regard to the means test and taking some of it back, there is something else I think is very unfair, if not deceiving. Perhaps before I go to that, I should say

to the government that one of the reasons I was particularly startled over these means test changes which are so inimical to the welfare of our older people is because they have done it before once or twice. When' it was done some years ago it was suggested to some of us through channels that are sometimes used that it was a mistake. Here it is being done again. I remind those who have been here long enough that in 1943, when Mr. Ilsley first raised the old age pension from $20 to $25 per month, he forgot to change the permissible income ceiling with the result it was reduced from $125 to $65.
The government made the same mistake in 1949 when it increased the pension from $30 to $40 per month. It did nothing about the permissible income ceilings, with the result that the other income that persons could earn was reduced from $20 a month for a single person to $10, and from $30 a month for a married couple to $5 each.
I think I can say, because after one has been around here a number of years one has experience on many committees and meets a lot of people, and even has cups of coffee with Liberals, and so on, that it was realized back in those years that what was done was a mistake; but it is being done again. It is being done again in these proposals which are not before us in this budget but which will be before us by means of the supplementary estimates to which the Minister of Finance made reference a moment ago. It is being done in the proposal that there be permissible income ceilings in some cases, namely in the case of the married recipients of old age assistance, the married recipients of the blindness allowance, and I presume-I have not seen these figures yet-married recipients of the disabled persons allowance. In their cases the permissible income is going up by an amount less thari the increase in the allowance, which has the effect of taking out of the pockets of those people, if they are married, $1 out of the magnanimous $6 which the Minister of Finance offered to these people on the night of his budget speech.
There is another trick that seems to me to make it impossible for any hon. member in this house to vote confidence in this government when this debate ends at a quarter to ten tonight. I suppose it is not too much of a surprise for the government to try to fool the people by talking about these pension increases becoming effective July 1, when it knows that that means July 31, but I do not think it is being completely fair with the Canadian people. Every time a government spokesman, a minister or a backbencher.

talks about these increases he refers to them as becoming effective on July 1. Technically, that is correct, but everyone who has had anything to do with these various benefit programs knows that the cheques are paid at the end of the month. The increase that is technically effective on July 1 will not be received by the recipients until July 31; sometimes the cheque is not received until the next day or two, which will make it August 1 or 2. Therefore the real effective date of these increases is not July 1, three weeks after the election, but July 31 or August 1, seven or eight weeks after the expected election date.
It does seem to us that if the government could not find a way to make pension increases commensurate with the rise in our gross national product, could not find a way to meet the figure which we have proposed, which has been voted down, or some other figure in between the government's $46 and the C.C.F. proposal for $75 a month, at least it could start by paying this miserly $6 increase sooner than July 31, or August 1.
I can tell the government that a good many letters which have come to me since these increases were announced, apart from the other things they say about the increases, do wonder why there cannot be an earlier increase. I wonder whether the Minister of Finance, I wonder whether government members know how many old age pensioners over 70 years of age have died since March 14, since the $6 increase was announced, without receiving it?
