speechtext: Silly.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Hon. members keep throwing in these interjections about melodrama and silliness. They do not realize how serious this problem is to the human beings we are talking about. On March 13, in answer to certain questions of mine, the government gave statistics which showed that in the 12 months of 1956 the number of old age pensioners over 70 who died was over 60,000. Our senior citizens over 70 in Canada pass on at the rate of 5,000 a month. By the law of averages, Mr. Speaker, 2,500 of our senior citizens 70 years of age and over have died since budget night without receiving the $6 increase.
The Budget-Mr. Knowles According to the figures given by the Minister of National Health and Welfare, or by his parliamentary assistant, on March 13, as can be found in Hansard of that date, 22,500 Canadians 70 years of age and over who on budget night learned that there was to be a $6 increase will have died before that increase is put into effect at the end of July or on August 1. I suggest that that kind of trickery, that kind of unfairness with Canada, that kind of unfairness with our senior citizens is such that this government deserves tonight at a quarter to ten the rebuke of the motion that is now before the house being defeated.
We in this party have talked about these things, pensions generally, pensions for our veterans and so on, not because they are part of the budget; they are not; they are not in the budget. The minister said by way of an interruption in my remarks that he would be tabling supplementary estimates later this week and I presume the house will have to find some way of dealing with them before the session ends. We have talked about old age pensions, pensions for the blind, pensions for disabled persons and for our war veterans, because the minister introduced these matters in his budget speech. But, I emphasize, they are not part of his budget. They are not part of what is before us in the motion now before the Chair. If and when some device is found at this session, as I hope it will be, to put these increases through so that they will be effective at the earliest possible date-I think they should be made effective immediately, certainly no later than May 1-the government will have our support; we will vote for the increases. We certainly do not approve of the ceilings in the case of the married persons, and we do not accept the amounts of increases as being adequate.
As a matter of fact, there is something to be said for this matter being dealt with by way of supplementary estimates; for that seems to leave the question of finality open until after the election. Perhaps it is well that it is being done that way, so that after the election we will not be saddled with $6 as the maximum amount of the increase, but so that we will be able to put through parliament a much more substantial increase for all of these groups of our citizens.
I say to the government, I say to parliament as a whole, if after the election is over we are on the other side of the house forming the government of this country there will be substantial increases in all of these pensions. If, perchance when the election is over we do not happen to be on the other side of the house but happen instead to be the official opposition I can tell the government that there will be prodding on these

The Budget-Mr. Huffman matters of the kind that an official opposition ought to give, something a lot stronger than the government has had in the last few years, the kind of prodding that will make action a necessity.
But these questions are not before us today. All that is before us today is a motion for Your Honour to leave the Chair for the house to go into committee of ways and means. If the motion carries and we get into committee of ways and means, with what will we be dealing? With pension increases? No. We will be dealing with budget resolutions and, as we in this group have already pointed out, the budget resolutions do not represent sound or sensible proposals. They do not come to grips with the financial or economic problems of the country. In other words the budget itself is not worth voting for and therefore we ask why should we bother going into committee of ways and means to deal with it at all?
In point of fact all that will be before the house tonight at a quarter to ten when this debate ends is the question as to whether or not this house has confidence in the government. This government has shown that it is inept and utterly unresponsive to the real needs of the human beings who compose this great country. The issue at the end of this debate is clear. Does this house have confidence in the kind of government that we have on the treasury benches at the present time? We say, "no."

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on this last day of the budget debate to take some time to commend the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) on the budget he has brought down and also to point out a few matters that I think should be looked into as time goes on.
The hon. member who has just taken his seat said that tonight at 9.45 this house will be asked to vote confidence in the government as represented by the hon. members sitting on the treasury benches. I am sure that newspapers express very well the ears, eyes and voices of the people of the respective communities they serve. A recent editorial which appeared in my own local newspaper said that the Minister of Finance's budget was a realistic budget having in mind all the phases of the growth and development of this great country of ours, to paraphrase its content.
I also rise at this time because of the remarks that were made last evening by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George

(Mr. Richardson) as they appear at the bottom of the first column of page 2937 of Hansard. He said:
One does not need to be a great student of economic affairs to say that if the farmers of western Canada, the fishermen on both coasts and in the inland waters of Canada, the trappers, those engaged in lumbering, if all these primary producers do not apply their labour to the natural resources of Canada we shall not long have economic well-being. Those of us who live in the city of Montreal just as those who live in the great city of Toronto or the city of Winnipeg . . . are particularly concerned and genuinely interested in those problems which are of immediate concern to miners, fishermen and all others throughout Canada whom we regard as primary producers.
I would like to commend the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George for his reference last evening to the primary producers. I think it reveals an excellent trend when an hon. member representing one of the ridings of the great metropolis of Montreal makes a remark such as was made in the speech to which I have just referred. I think it augurs well for the future of agriculture and the primary producers when the people living in the city are taking note that the primary producers must have a full share in the natural growth of this country and enjoy all the progress that other segments of our population are enjoying. Because of the interest displayed by people in the cities I am sure that this condition will come about.
I would like to make one suggestion, and it is this. Practically every service club throughout this country has what they call a rural-urban night. On these occasions the primary producers such as those referred to by the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George sit down with the people who represent business, finance and industry and engage in consultation and discussion of their problems. I suggest that such activities should be encouraged.
I do not know of any better way by which people living in cities can learn of the conditions that prevail among the primary producers and I am sure that with the full understanding that can be gained through associations of that kind the urban people will help the primary producers achieve the goal that is so necessary for the full development of this country and its continued prosperity.
As a farmer in my own right I would like to point out one matter in particular which has affected the income of farmers during the past year. In my own area last year we had a rather backward and wet spring. The summer was far too cool to produce the type of crops that we normally produce in the best manner. At the end of the growing season frost occurred much earlier than usual and the result was that the net return to the producers in my area was much lower than it would have been if we had had normal

weather and a normal growing season. I know from personal experience that many of our people have experienced the same difficulty I did on my own property. Those who have been engaged in farming for many years realize that this is a normal situation which occurs every so often and for that reason they accept it as a matter of consequence and are looking forward to a better season this coming year.
In his opening remarks a brief while ago the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe (Mr. Rowe) said something to the effect that this government follows along, is essentially a follower. I do know that this government has followed the recommendations which have been made from time to time by the commodity groups which have come here to make representations. I commend the government for taking the advice of those people who are primarily interested in this type of effort.
Then again the hon. member for Dufferin-Simcoe said that he was in favour of a degree of parity prices. I think there is quite a difference between what some of the members here feel in regard to parity prices and what was expressed by the provincial minister of agriculture when speaking in London to a group only this past week. The minister had this to say, that he did not believe in parity prices, but following his address he cleared up the point by saying it would be extremely difficult, if not impossible, to set fair parity prices and he questioned whether they could be established. In this same address the minister of agriculture for Ontario said that the future of farmers is bright, and I quite agree that we have reached the low point as far as agriculture is concerned. I do agree with the minister of agriculture for Ontario and I do agree with the Minister of Agriculture for Canada that these things which we have experienced during this past while are things of the past and that we will enjoy, as the minister of agriculture for Ontario says, a greater share of the natural wealth than we are enjoying at the present time.
One of the things that I would like to mention and which I think can be of particular value, especially in the area from which I come, is this: On the last budget I spoke about the difference in freight rates that apply to United States corn coming into this country, United States soybeans coming into this country and going over Canadian-owned roads and delivered at processing plants in Canada, which, on a mileage rate, is much more favourable to the United States products. Again, and only briefly, I would like to suggest to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Marler) that this problem might be 82715-188J
The Budget-Mr. Huffman referred to the board of transport commissioners to be reviewed and I am sure that something would be done that would be to>
the betterment of the producers of these commodities in the southern tip of Ontario.
Another thing that enters into the picture as far as the prices of these commodities are concerned at the present time is the strong position of the Canadian dollar. There-is a tariff of 8 cents against corn coming into-this country, but on the basis of the present price and the strong position of the Canadian-dollar that tariff is reduced to almost 3 cents in place of the 8 cents that was established. I quite agree that we all take a lot of satisfaction from the fact that our economy is such that it commends itself to the higher dollar value.
I was very pleased the other day when the-Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) made the-statement in the house with regard to the-marketing legislation. The farm organizations from our part of the country and all of Ontario which were here placed a very sound argument before a committee of the cabinet, and by their representations sought to have an amendment made in relation to farm marketing legislation. In our own area I presume that it is more highly organized than any other part of this country because we have so many specialized groups. We feel in our area that it would be impossible to carry on with the farm marketing organizations without the amending legislation that was proposed. I have heard on the floor of this house statements by members of the government commending some of our organizations to other commodity groups because they had been most useful organizations in helping to bring about orderly marketing and good conditions within the groups which they served.
I would like, for a few moments now, to indicate that I feel that the freight rate structure should be carefully analysed and for this reason. Out of every 100 tillable acres across my county, 21 acres are devoted to corn. In one township alone 35 acres out of every 100 tillable acres are devoted to the production of corn. On a survey of the elevators which handled cereal crops in our area in this past year it was found that 55 per cent of the cash realized from the sale of cereal products was realized from the production of corn, and so I think you will see how important it would be to us if the freight rate structure was fully analysed and if it was realistic in relation to other commodities; also that United States corn would not have an advantage on a per mile rate basis.
Before I resume my seat I would just like to refer to the statement that was made

The Budget-Mr. Huffman [DOT] on March 30 by the member for Lambton West (Mr. Murphy) who had this to say, in referring to the travel bureau:
I submit that if we cannot do any better than that we should scrap the travel bureau and give [DOT]this money to the provinces in proportion to their ,population.
I would like to commend the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Xesage) for the way in which the travel ibureau has advertised Canada in the United States.

Mr. Speaker,. I rise really to offer an explanation of our position in respect to this bill and as it might apply to other bills. There are a number of divorce bills on the order paper and the time availabe for private members' bills is expiring very rapidly. We feel that perhaps it is not just fair to those people who have paid their money, whose cases have been heard and who have been granted these divorces. There may be some reason why they should not be granted, but it does appear to us that there may be some strategy on the part of some hon. members to hold up these divorces for some other reason.
If the other reason is that the TransMountain Pipe Line bill should not come before the house it would mean that those people who are interested in these divorce cases will have to pay the price for the TransMountain Pipe Line bill not going through. We think that is not fair, and if the pipe line bill is not to go through it could be talked

Private Bills-Divorce
out. We do not believe that these people who have paid their money, and gone through all the divorce proceedings in the other place, should be the victims of that.
We have been voting with our colleagues to our right on these cases as a protest against this particular method of handling divorce bills. We do in this matter appeal now for some fairness. We could abstain from voting; we could go out of the house or we could vote the other way. However, it will take just as much time, so we will not be saving anything even if we did those things. I suppose we will continue to vote as a protest to this method, but I think we should appeal to the judgment of all members now and not have these people the victims of any strategy, if there is any strategy in it.

I should like to congratulate the hon. member for Macleod (Mr. Hansell) for the very fair remarks he has made concerning this matter. Apparently there are some tactics being resorted to, and I should like to question the propriety of any member in the house or any group in the house resorting to these sort of tactics which, in simple language, are a waste of time, a waste of parliament's time, a waste of the country's time and a waste of the country's money. If there is something factual, if there is something realistic, if there is a principle involved, I think hon. members owe it to the house and owe it to the country to say why they resort to these tactics. Apparently there is some reason that these gentlemen will not disclose to the country for resorting to these tactics.
It is unfair to hon. members in the house and if it were possible at all to censure hon. members for resorting to these tactics, certainly such a censure should be imposed. If the house lacks the authority to impose such a censure, the facts should be drawn to the attention of the country so that in due time the country may impose a censure upon any group that resorts to these kind of unfair tactics wasting the country's time and money.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, because of the relatively limited opportunity at this session to discuss matters of urgent importance to one's own constituency which, while particular, are but symptoms of situations that have larger implications, I should like to follow a course this evening which I have not usually followed on the budget debate, and bring to the attention of the government and the house certain difficulties in my own constituency rather than to devote the whole of my remarks to the budget itself. I should like to refer particularly to the situation confronting our cattle growers with respect to the difficulty in obtaining supplies of feed grains at reasonable prices; and to the problems of Columbia river power development.
But before doing so I should like to say a word or two in general about' the budget. A number of attempts have been made both in the house and outside to give a name to this budget. I recall it being defined as "the bubble gum budget" or "the sugar candy budget", and other uncomplimentary terms have been used with respect to the efforts of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris). But I would rather approach the budget on a different basis. I prefer rather to define it in terms of what it does and what it does not do and also to give credit to the Minister of Finance where credit is due for the efforts he has made and to suggest blame where blame is attachable and offer some particular criticisms.
Approaching the budget on that basis, I would say that the minister seems to have taken to heart some of the lectures which he has been given in the press of Canada, mainly in the press friendly to the government. I think particularly of such journals as the Winnipeg Free Press and also articles written by another journalist friend of the government, Mr. Bruce Hutchison, where the minister has been warned that if he is to retain the respect of the Liberal party, as interpreted and defined by the Free Press and Mr. Hutchison he must be consistent.

The Budget-Mr. Fulton He has been told that, having sounded warnings as he has of the dangerous implications *of the present economic situation and having sounded the praises as he has of the policy of high taxes and surpluses, he should stick to those policies.
I give the minister credit generally speaking, for having been consistent in the budget that he presented to the house some two or three weeks ago. He did indeed try to be consistent with those policies which he has advocated and followed over the past few years.
For instance, as a result of the minister's policies we have had very high taxes. He obviously felt that it was the part of consistency to keep taxes high. He certainly succeeded. He has kept taxes at record high levels. Again over the past years the minister followed a policy which did not allow him to permit the average Canadian to keep for himself, after he had paid his taxes, any surplus of his own earnings for his own requirements. The minister seemed determined to continue to disallow Canadians from keeping their own earnings, and in this respect he has succeeded in being consistent.
Indeed, the minister has succeeded admirably in maintaining a consistent policy of applying the screws to the average Canadian taxpayer so that after the end of the year when he has met his own day to day living requirements and paid his taxes he has virtually nothing left over.
Along with high taxation, the minister has also followed a policy in past years of the accumulation of substantial surpluses, apparently based upon the belief-we have to recognize the belief and, as I say, give credit for consistency where consistency is shown-that spending of the people's money by the government is better than spending of the people's money by the people themselves and that, somehow, record high levels of government expenditure are less inflationary, although generally speaking nonproductive, than it would be to allow the people to keep their own money for their own purposes, to save for their own future and invest in the development of Canada. So the minister has ended the fiscal years, with one notable exception, with substantial surpluses, and he has certainly been consistent this year and has forecast an equally consistent program for next year.
Indeed, in the analysis of the budget as a whole we must, while giving credit for consistency, suggest that the minister is open to the criticism that he has given no recognition in this year's budget, more than he has in the past, to the problem of the average Canadian who would like, and who, IMr. Fulton.]

indeed, we on this side believe is entitled, to end up the year with some savings, some surplus himself. You see, Mr. Speaker, attention has been focused to such an extent upon the surplus accumulated by the government that we have been inclined to forget the right of the Canadian taxpayer to end up the year with his own surplus. As a result he has been placed in a position where it is absolutely impossible for him to do so.
There have been a number of justifications advanced as to why the tax rate should be kept high and why surpluses should be confined to governments rather than to taxpayers. We are told that high taxes and budgetary surpluses are anti-inflationary. We are also told that there are a number of other justifications for high taxes such as that they are a method of redistributing income and wealth. It is interesting to analyse these justifications briefly. There was an old and, I have always felt, healthy doctrine, that taxes were only justified to the extent that they enabled government to meet its actual financial commitments, that they were a painful necessity but that government was entitled to take from the people through taxes what it required to meet its actual financial commitments.
But now there are these interesting new justifications for high taxes-that they are anti-inflationary or that they are a method of redistributing income. Well, it is interesting to recall that in the majority of years since the end of the war we have had high taxes, and substantial surpluses: but we still have mounting inflation, we still have some very rich people and we still have some very poor people. Indeed, I suggest that we have a new group of poor people, namely the tax-poor. There is an increasing number of Canadians who end up the year on April 30-having met their own increasing living costs and having paid their taxes- with absolutely nothing left over with which to meet any emergency. Confronted with the emergency of unexpected sickness, accident or any other sort of emergency, they have nothing left with which to meet it and they are driven into the hands of the finance companies. It is interesting to reflect upon the growth of the finance companies in Canada over the recent years. I was in a small, average Canadian city the other day and I was told that whereas about four or five years ago that city had one finance company, it now has nine.
What about the Canadian who wants to save for his own future or to invest in the future development of Canada? What opportunity has he at the end of the fiscal year when the government has collected from him

the taxes with which it accumulates its own surplus? What surplus is left to the average Canadian to invest in the development of Canada? There is none because of the government's policy that it and it alone is entitled to accumulate surpluses.
The minister has accumulated a surplus of $400 million or more this year in spite of the various efforts he has made to hide it. He has a surplus that would have meant $100 to the average Canadian family with which to save or to invest, or five cents an hour in take-home pay to the average Canadian wage earner that he might have had at the end of the year to save or to invest or to meet emergencies with which he might be confronted.
In respect of all this we must admit that the minister has been consistent and that he has not changed his policy. We must admit that with the limits he allowed himself for tax relief, he recognized that he had only very limited fields in which to give concessions. I said I would give credit where credit is due. I must give the minister credit for the fact that, within the limits thus allowed to him, he has spread his concessions with what I must call a blatant cynicism. I recall what happened in the course of delivering his budget, while he was doing his best to spread the concessions with a thin smear, as I might call it, over as many as he might be able to reach. After having announced some three, four or five of these trifling concessions, when he came to the next one he was greeted with laughter; and the minister just simply could not refrain from laughing himself because he knew just how cynical was his whole approach.

As to those concessions that were given, it is obvious that they were given with one object in view and that was, as I have said, to touch lightly as many Canadians as possible. They were given on a most unscientific basis. It seemed to me that the approach of the minister was that having taken his hands out of as few as possible of the taxpayers' pockets, he was going to put his hand back into as many pockets as possible in terms of concessions. The result was that with few exceptions the concessions mean virtually nothing. Particularly they mean nothing to those who really needed them.
In no field is this fact more conspicuous than in the field of old age pensions. On all sides of the house since the budget speech was
The Budget-Mr. Fulton delivered we have had occasion to realize the bitter disappointment felt by the old age-pensioners. Of some particular significance-is it to find that absolutely without exception the social welfare agencies which are interested in this problem, not from the point of view of votes but because they know the real need on the part of many old age pensioners, were bitterly disappointed by the minister's approach to the problem of increases in old age pensions. I would suggest that there is no greater proof of the cynicism with which this problem has been approached' than the fact that the increases have been delayed until July 1.

speechtext: Whether it be July 1 or July 31, the fact is that the budget was announced in March. There is no administrative problem here of any insuperable nature which would have made it impossible to give the increase by May 1 at the latest, if not April 1. There is only one reason that I can suggest or indeed that anyone can possibly see for the increases having been delayed as they are. That reason is that there is to be an election between now and the date when the increases become effective. We have seen it in the approach which the party of my hon. friends opposite are making to the people now. They are going to try to tell them this: Unless you vote Liberal in the election, you will not get your old age pension increase.

speechtext:
What other possible reason-can there have been for delaying the increase until after the date of the election? If one of my hon. friends opposite who are now growling and grumbling can give me a good reason, I should be glad to hear it. But there is not one who can give a good reason because there is no good reason for that delay beyond the explanation that I have suggested. I therefore submit to you, Mr. Speaker, that in summary this budget can be described as one of the most cynical approaches that we have yet seen in this house to the two problems of relief to Canadian taxpayers and assistance to Canadians who are genuinely in need of social security benefits.

The Budget-Mr. Fulton
I should now like to turn to the two specific problems which I mentioned at the beginning. Perhaps I should deal first with the question of power development in British Columbia. This matter is not unrelated to the budget, Mr. Speaker, because you will recall that in his budget speech the minister reversed the previous trend of government policy and said that the federal government Is now prepared to offer assistance to provinces with respect to the development of power projects where they were satisfied that the development is justifiable. This represents a complete reversal of government policy; and that reversal, I suggest, is dictated by the approach of the election.
Although we in this house, confronted with the rigors and unpleasantness of election campaigns, sometimes dread an election, nevertheless it is interesting to contemplate the number of benefits-even though sometimes restricted-the elections actually bring. Sometimes I think it might be a healthy thing if elections were held more often because they sometimes produce refreshing changes in government policy, and projects which have been refused consistently in years between elections, suddenly assume an attractiveness in the eyes of the government and bring forth promises of assistance on the eve of an election.
In no respect is this trend more significant than in connection with this matter of power development. Here I should say that I am going to deal specifically with the problem of the Columbia river in British Columbia. You will recall that on Monday of last week, the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Sinclair) made an announcement in British Columbia. Incidentally, I should point out and emphasize that it was not made in this house although this house has shown continuing interest in the problem and is entitled to be informed as soon as is anybody else. But the minister made the announcement in Vancouver in the course of an election or pre-election visit. He announced that the federal government is now prepared to assist the province of British Columbia with respect to the development of power on the Columbia river. Here are the words of the Minister of Fisheries as restated by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Lesage) on March 26, 1957 at page 2684 of Hansard:
If, after international agreement has been reached, the provincial government should decide on public development of this great power potential and need assistance in financing, the federal government will 'be prepared to assist in the same way that it has joined with the government of Ontario-
This represents a complete reversal of government policy. May I say, of course,

immediately, that that announcement is welcomed particularly by every member from British Columbia, as I know it will be by every member in the house and by each province. But it does represent a complete reversal of government policy, and it is interesting to note the timing of the announcement.
Last year, as we have every year over the past four or five years, the official opposition introduced an amendment having to do with the development of natural resources in Canada. We introduced a similar amendment this year. I shall analyse the record of the government in connection with that amendment in a moment. But in addition to the general amendment on national development, last year we introduced a specific amendment having to do with the development of power resources in these terms, as found at page 1346 of Hansard for February 20, 1956:
In the opinion of this house consideration should be given to a joint investment program for the development of power resources in any province where the government of such province requests the co-operation of the Canadian government in carrying out such development.
This amendment was introduced by Mr. Drew, then leader of the opposition. It was supported by the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra (Mr. Green), the hon. member for Prince Albert (Mr. Diefenbaker), as he then was, now Leader of the Opposition. In the course of their speeches specific reference was made to the possibility of a joint development program on the Columbia river. It is interesting to note, that on February 21 the government as a whole, including significantly the Minister of Fisheries, voted against that motion. They voted against a motion calling upon the government to enter into a joint investment program for the development of power resources in any province where the government of such province requests the cooperation of the Canadian government in carrying out such developments.
This year, on February 11, the Leader of the Opposition introduced a general resolution regarding a national development policy. In the course of his speech, he made the following remarks, as reported at page 1159 of Hansard for that date, and I might emphasize that he was speaking in support of the resolution on national development when he stated specifically:
We believe that there should be formulated a federal power policy in voluntary co-operation with such provinces as desire it in order to assure a continuing expansion of low-cost energy in Canada. Such a policy would help create, if asked for by the province of British Columbia, a huge industrial empire there-
It is interesting to note that on February 11 of this year every member of the government present in the house voted against that

motion, a motion which called upon the government to assist, if asked by the province of British Columbia, in the development of power projects in that province. This, then, is the record up until February 11 of this year of the government who, by its spokesman the Minister of Fisheries, announced in Vancouver on March 25 that the federal government is now prepared to assist if the provincial government should decide on public development and need assistance in financing. It is an interesting reversal of policy, and the timing is particularly interesting and significant. It is amazing what a change of heart the imminence of an election can bring about upon the part of this government.
As I have said, we welcome the change of heart. But I believe it is not too much to suggest or to ask the Canadian people when they are assessing this whole situation that they conclude for themselves from which government they are most likely to get real assistance and progress in these matters. Is it likely to come from the government which has had a change of heart only on the eve of an election and makes its pronouncement in the course of an election campaign and which, of course, has shown a remarkable but unfortunate readiness to forget about its election promises once an election is over? On the other hand, would they expect greater chances of a real implementation of the policy from a party which believes in that policy and which has had a national development policy as the very core of its program ever since the party came into existence, and which has stuck to that policy and implemented it whenever given the opportunity to do so? I do not think the people of my province will be deluded by this change of heart on the part of this government into believing they are going to get any more from these promises than they have been able to get from this government in the years gone by.
There is one most unfortunate matter that must be mentioned in this connection and that is the utterly irresponsible attitude of the Minister of Fisheries with regard to the proposed diversion of part of the Columbia river waters into the Fraser river system. As I pointed out the other day, there are at the present time delicate and important negotiations going on between the government of Canada and the government of the United States with respect to downstream benefits, which could mean a return to Canada for the development of power on the United States side of the boundary made possible by storage development on the Canadian side of the boundary in the Columbia river. It will be recalled by the house, as a result of previous discussions of this matter, that there
The Budget-Mr. Fulton is also the most interesting and fascinating possibility that at one and the same site, Mica creek on the Columbia river, we can develop enormous power potential and also enormous storage potential, and that the release of these stored waters would of course benefit power installations already completed on the United States side of the boundary as well as our own. What we are now negotiating under the terms of the international boundary waters treaty, is what returns should be given to Canada for the increased power development made possible on the United States side as a result of the Canadian storage of water.
We are, of course, in an infinitely superior bargaining position with respect to these negotiations, if we can say, as General McNaughton has put us in the position of saying, that unless the Americans are willing to agree to a satisfactory return to Canada in return for the downstream benefits which they receive we shall exercise our right to divert those storage waters through the diversion of the Columbia into the Fraser river system and thus generate further power in Canada on the Fraser river system. The possibility of the Columbia diversion into the Fraser is an enormously important matter to British Columbia particularly, and to Canada, with respect to the negotiations about to begin with the United States government on this whole question of downstream benefits on the Columbia river.
What do we find? We find that the Minister of Fisheries is busy doing his best to throw away this lever which Canada has with respect to those negotiations, because even before the detailed negotiations commence he has publicly stated in Vancouver that he is opposed to the Columbia diversion. He talks about it in terms of relieving the threat to the Fraser river fisheries, saving the Fraser river fisheries from the threat of power development. These words refer specifically to the Columbia river diversion. So you have a position where the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources is entering into negotiation with the United States, in the course of which he would have a tremendous lever, if the Canadian government would preserve that lever with respect to the possible Columbia diversion. You have that minister on the one hand, but on the other you have the Minister of Fisheries from British Columbia doing all he can to prejudice the success of those negotiations with respect to one of the biggest bargaining weapons that we have. That, sir, is irresponsibility in the extreme.
I asked the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) about it the other day; I asked him what remained of the principle of cabinet solidarity in this respect, and you recall what the reply of the right hon. gentleman was. He
2988	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Fulton said, "I think this debate has gone on long enough". That, of course, is the kind of answer that we get from this government because, as we have seen so clearly in the course of past debates in this house and developments in that connection-the pipe line debate, I think of particularly-this government does not believe in any of the principles that we used to regard as the principles governing the course of democratic government in Canada. It no longer believes in the principle of the supremacy of parliament, and it obviously does not subscribe to the principle of cabinet solidarity. This is not just an academic question; this is a question of Canada's vital interests which are being prejudiced by the irresponsibility of the present government.
I would like now to refer briefly to the other problem that confronts my province and particularly the cattle growers in my constituency, namely the problem of obtain-ning a supply of feed grain at reasonable prices. I am glad to see the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) here because I want to place it before him and his colleague, the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). We have discussed it briefly in previous exchanges in this house, and the right hon. gentlemen and I have had correspondence about the matter. I regret that to date we do not seem to have been able to arrive at any sort of satisfactory solution, and perhaps it would be fair to state we have not even yet achieved a reasonable meeting of minds.
I appreciate the fact that the government is committed to-and indeed we have supported-the principle of the wheat board method of marketing grain. In my discussion with the British Columbia beef cattle growers association and the British Columbia livestock producers co-operative association they have made it clear to me, and I state it unequivocally here, that they are anxious not to do anything which would jeopardize the wheat board system of marketing grain. But there is a legitimate interest on the part of our beef producers in British Columbia, approximately 85 per cent to 90 per cent of whom are represented by the association I have mentioned. They have a legitimate interest in obtaining adequate supplies of feed grain at reasonable prices, and particularly in obtaining feed grains at prices comparable with the prices for feed grain which the producers of cattle on the prairies have to pay. At the present time-and I have checked the figures and rechecked them with the association-they have to pay for grain delivered in Williams Lake, to mention one point


only, anything varying from wheat at $59.78 a ton to barley at $52.04 a ton. That was February 13, 1957.

speechtext: I have never questioned that; that is correct.

But they find-and I have verified this-that the growers of cattle on the prairies are able to obtain supplies of grain from their neighbours who grow grain at prices varying from $20 to $25 a ton.
You will appreciate, and the whole house will appreciate, that since our cattle have to compete on the Vancouver market with grain-fed cattle from the prairies, and since the trend is almost universal today to grain-fed cattle, that places our cattle growers in a terrible competitive position.

I have never quarrelled with that statement; it is not the wheat board's price. But I have seen advertisements, I have been shown advertisements in the prairie papers, carried by people who really have never been in this business before advertising that they will take cattle and supply grain on feed lots at prices which, as I have said, run around the figure I have mentioned, $20 to $25 a ton.
It may well be that this situation will be acute only in years of surplus grain production; but it is in years of surplus grain production that agriculture seems to get into difficulties, and it is in those years that depressed prices and uncertain economic conditions in the agriculture industry most affect the cattle producers of British Columbia.

speechtext: I hoped that I might just lay the problem before the minister before getting into a direct contradiction in views. I can only repeat to him through you, sir, what I have said earlier, that I have had these prices checked and double-checked. These are not the prices of frozen grain; they may not be the prices of No. 1, or first grade grain, but they are the prices at which feeders of cattle on the prairies are able to obtain supplies of perfectly adequate feed grains from their neighbours.

speakerposition: Minister of Agriculture
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Any man who lives on the prairies knows you are not right except in occasional cases.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I hold in my hand a suggestion from the livestock co-operative association of British Columbia of a method which might solve the problem of our producers and at the same time preserve the wheat board marketing system of grain. They say:
What is needed now is some formula under which any farmer or farmers' association in Alberta, who wishes to sell grain by direct dealing to a farmer or farmers' association in British Columbia, can do so at an agreed price.
The minister has mentioned difficulty in following through a particular lot of grain once it has entered an elevator and we must admit that grain can be handled more economically through elevators in most cases.
I would suggest a procedure something along the following lines.
Brown in British Columbia wishes to buy Number 2 feed oats from Jones in Alberta and they reach an agreement on price. Brown fills out a form, signed also by acceptable witnesses of his bona fides, certifying that he needs the grain to feed to his own stock.
In other words, it is not for resale.
If instead of Brown the buyer is an association or farmers' institute they certify that the grain will be fed only to their members' stock.
Jones-
The grower on the prairies-
-takes this form to his local elevator which applies to the wheat board for permission to ship the number of carloads specified in the agreement between Jones and Brown to Brown, on delivery of an equivalent amount of Number 2 feed oats from Jones.
Payment will be made direct from Brown to Jones, but the elevator's handling charges will be deducted from their eventual settlement with Jones when his consignment of No. 2 feed oats is sold.
They point out that no legislation should be needed to accomplish this, only a regulation by the wheat board exempting such transactions made under permit so that the grain from the prairies could be shipped to the purchaser in British Columbia and receive the feed grain assistance now available.
They conclude with this comment which I submit for the consideration of the minister:
The only time when such a scheme would not work to the advantage of all farmers, elevators and board, would be when there is a shortage of box cars; these "permit shipments" would then have to wait until the shortage had been overcome.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the budget has received a rather thorough going over and it is not my intention to repeat the things that have been said about it. However there are a few matters which have not yet received much if any attention and after dealing at short length with one or two matters on which I should like to simply restate our position I would like to deal with these new subjects for just a few minutes before summarizing the stand that we take with regard to the vote that is coming in a matter of an hour from now.
The first subject I would like to discuss just briefly is the question of succession duties. I would like to tell the minister again-for perhaps he has been told several times already -that a good many thousand of Canadian citizens and particularly our womenfolk were bitterly disappointed that the minister failed to indicate in his budget any change in succession duties this year. It seems to me that the Canadian people had every right to expect the government would bring in amendments to the act this year to bring up to date the provisions contained in the old act. As a matter of fact the present act is not only outmoded but it appears that it must have been drafted and conducted through parliament by people who considered the Canadian housewife as a chattel. Certainly they did not give any indication that they believed she was a person. I find now that womenfolk throughout the whole country are up in arms and have their tomahawks bared and are after the minister's scalp. I cannot blame them because they feel they should have better treatment and I think they should too.
We in this group very strongly support their demands. I think they are reasonable demands. They ask that half of a deceased husband's estate be considered for tax purposes as having been earned by his widow and therefore should not be subject to succession duties when it passes to her upon the death of her husband. This is of particular importance to farming people. The wives of farmers have contributed in no small way to the building up of the estate and they should have that consideration.
The second claim they make is that instead of exempting estates up to $50,000, as is the practice now, this amount should be made a true exemption deductible from the value of the estate before the calculation of succession duties.
There is one more demand that is being made today and which has considerable merit. It is that half of the value of a gift of
2990	HOUSE OF
The Budget-Mr. Low
property or of any other nature from a husband to a wife be not subject to the gift tax; that is to say only half of the value should be subject to tax and the other half should not be so taxed.
Canada must be looked upon by other nations as a country which is just emerging from the stone age if we are to be judged by the present succession duty act under which we have been operating in this country for so many years. I hope the minister will not lose any time in bringing in amendments which will render the act more up to date than do the provisions he has made.
Much has been said about old age pensions and it is not my intention to engage in a lengthy discussion of the subject. I think I should state as others have, however, that I feel ashamed of the very meagre increase of $6 a month provided by the minister especially in the light of what was said this afternoon by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). The minister could very easily have made the amount of increase $20 a month and in my judgment not less than that is required to meet the increase in the cost of living since 1949. I have not too much of an axe to grind in the matter because in my province we are already providing $55 a month and in the other Social Credit province of British Columbia they are providing a supplementary payment of $20 a month.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: You are providing $15.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Yes, that is true. To be exact I should have said that in my province of Alberta we are providing a supplementary allowance of $15 a month which brings the total to $55 so that any increase this government would make now would not add too much to what I have already suggested is the required minimum to meet the present cost of living. It seems to me that if the minister were to exercise what I believe is the fertile brain and imagination he has in his head he could figure out ways and means of putting into the hands of the aged citizens of this country the surpluses of food, clothing, fuel and other materials that are present in abundance so that these people could have a decent standard of living.
There is another matter in connection with old age pensions with which the government should have dealt long ago. I believe I have not heard anyone mention it during this present session. I see no real reason why it should be necessary to continue to apply the 20-year residence rule before aged citizens are eligible for pensions. The people who come to Canada and have every intention of remaining here to make their contribution
[Mr. Low.l

as good citizens should not be required to wait 20 years before they become eligible for pensions. There are many people in this country who are 75, 80 and even 85 years of age and who are experiencing great difficulty in making a living. No one will hire them and in most cases they have not had the good fortune to lay by very much on which they could eke out a meagre existence for a period of years but they cannot participate in our old age pension scheme because they have not resided in this country for 20 years. It seems to me we should give them treatment commensurate with the treatment we accord immigrants who bring their children to this country. After one year's residence the children of immigrants become eligible for receipt of the family allowance payments. Why in the world should we treat one group in one fashion and a second group in a different way? I believe we would be doing only what is right if we were to make it possible for aged people who had not been residents of Canada for 20 years and who, as I have said, have made their homes here and contributed to the building up of this country, to have at least a modicum of the security provided under the Old Age Pensions Act.
There is another matter related to old age pensions which I think we ought to attend to as well, and it is this.
Industry looks with disfavour on retaining in employment or taking on into new employment anyone beyond 55 or 60 years of age. They want younger people and they seem to be, many of them, in a dreadful hurry to retire men and women who although they have reached 65 years of age nevertheless are still in excellent physical condition and capable of many more years of active and useful work. People age faster in these days, in this modern age of speed, and it is becoming harder year by year for middle-aged people to find a decent job. Increasing mechanization, or what we call automation, is going to make it all the harder. Governments, it is my judgment, will of necessity have to adopt lower pensionable ages if suffering is to be prevented and if the goods and services that our economy produces are to find their way into the hands of the people who need them. From an economic point of view alone I think it is essential that we make an immediate and thorough study of the whole question of pensionable ages, with a view to doing something about it soon; as a humanitarian problem it is most urgent.
Now a related problem is that of a nationwide transferable pension plan for workers. The workers are finding it increasingly difficult as they are laid off work in a branch of industry to find security in any other job

and many times commerce and industry will not take into their employment people who have lost a job in another branch of industry and who have not some way of carrying on with their pension arrangements. That in itself makes it more difficult for people in the later years of their lives to find decent employment. It seems to me that we ought to be doing something about it in this country. I understand that Beardsley Ruml in the United States has drafted a proposed plan for the national planning association there. I understand the plan is now before the Congress of the United States for study and I would certainly recommend to the government that something be done about the problem here.
When parliament meets again I think it would be advisable to have the industrial relations committee of this house take up a study of such a nation-wide transferable pension plan for all the workers of Canada. It is not beyond the bounds of possibility that we could find something that would work and certainly it would be of tremendous assistance to the people of the country who find it necessary to transfer, during their middle age perhaps, from one job in industry or commerce to another.
For a few moments I would like to turn to the consideration of a matter which in my judgment, is of sufficient importance to warrant a most earnest and searching study by members of the government and I mean particularly the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent), the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Pearson), the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) and the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. McCann). This matter involves an attempt by United States tax collectors to reach over into Canada for the purpose of collecting twelve years of back taxes on income and capital growth of a Canadian company, income on which Canadian taxes to the extent of between $600,000 and $700,000 have already been paid under Canadian law.
It appears that the United States internal revenue department is seeking to collect $2,598,000 from Premium Iron Ores Limited on income which it claims the company earned during the war years. That was a period when the Canadian government thought it was to the national interest, and I thought it was, to grant exemptions both to Steep Rock iron ores and Premium Iron Ores Limited for the purpose of encouraging them to develop ore beds so as to make it possible for both Canada and the United States to put on a real war effort. At the time the United States was becoming short of iron ore, at least it thought it was, and in order to assure itself of ample supplies it co-operated
The Budget-Mr. Low
with Canada in giving encouragement to these two particular companies, to help them to get started.
Here are some of the facts which ought to be most carefully considered and I put them on the record because I am concerned about what this case may lead to. The United States government is demanding that Premium Iron Ores Limited pay approximately $2,600,000 back taxes and at the same time they demand that the owners of Premium Iron Ores, who are United States citizens, pay another $2 million in personal taxes. The basis of the United States government's claim against Premium is that it says Premium Iron Ores had a permanent office in the United States and therefore it is liable for income tax. One of the major owners of Premium Iron Ores Limited, Cyrus Eaton, says that this company did not at any time have a permanent office in the United States and therefore does not owe the tax. In fact, the owners of the company say that the Canadian corporation had no office or bank account, offices, directors or employees in the United States, the corporation conducted no business in the United States and it neither purchased nor sold anything in the United States. It had no contracts either, with any United States company.
Premium Iron Ores Limited is a Canadian registered company and is sales agent for Steep Rock Iron Mines Limited. There is in existence today, as members of the government know, a tax treaty between Canada and the United States which is designed to avoid double taxation. The United States revenue department takes the position, however, that the Premium case has nothing whatever to do with the supplementary convention to the United States-Canada tax treaty which is now under consideration by the senate foreign relations committee of congress.
Now Premium makes the claim, which in my judgment is of tremendous interest to Canada, that the United States tax action against it, and Mr. Eaton and Mr. Daley his partner, private United States citizens, jeopardizes the tax treaty between our two countries and makes it possible for similar Canadian companies to be slapped with back taxes by the United States bureau of internal revenue. The United States says for its part that there is no principle involved such as this and that it is only interested in Premium and in no other companies. However, I think I can see a good many indications which would lead me to believe just the reverse. In the meantime the Premium case is now before the United States tax court; how long it will be there of course is anybody's guess, but it should not take too long to solve the case.
The joint committee of the internal revenue taxation in the United States is aware that

The Budget-Mr. Low
the Canadian government has not protested the internal revenue's action against Premium Iron Ores Limited. This appears to be considered by the committee as a very important point. The United States state department has already said that it is wrong to think the action of the United States internal revenue department against Premium is a unilateral action. It says that Ottawa has never challenged the United States attempt to collect tax and some of the officials indicate that they feel that silence on Canada's part indicates acceptance or at least non-objection by this country.
Now the Prime Minister some months ago -I do not know the exact date but I know that he did some months ago, and of course he admitted this a few days ago in answer to my question-sent an aide-memoire to the United States government saying that the co-operation which the Canadian tax officials gave to the United States tax officials in gathering information on the Premium case did not mean the approval of the United States position in that case. Now I say that that is not a protest by any stretch of the imagination. It is reported also that the memoire said that when the Canadian government, as a war measure to increase essential production, agreed to exempt Premium from income and excess profits taxes for the period of three years it was not contemplated that there would be any United States tax applicable to these operations of the company which the Canadian and the United States governments were both trying to accelerate in the joint interests of their two countries.
From the Prime Minister's reply to my question on Tuesday, March 19, it appears that he is under the impression that the Premium Iron Ores tax case involves only the question of permanent establishment. There appears also to be the impression in official circles in Canada that the "permanent establishment" claim is a question of fact which should be committed to the courts for determination. I say, Mr. Speaker, that is not the case, and we have to look at it that way. An international group of accountants, lawyers and technicians has made a most searching and careful study of this whole situation and in their report they make, amongst others, this very potent statement:
The action taken by the United States taxing authorities in assessing taxes against Premium Iron Ores reveals a basic policy determination by the United States officials which amounts to a virtual rewriting of the treaty. The treaty was designed to prevent double taxation of all industrial and commercial profits excepting cases where the corporation was engaged in substantial business at a fixed, definite, and permanent establishment in both countries.

They continue:
The Premium case discloses that the United States taxing authorities have adopted the policy of seizing upon slight, insubstantial, and isolated activities as a basis for asserting that the Canadian companies have a permanent establishment in the United States and for imposing United States taxes upon them. The case demonstrates that the United States authorities have decided, as a matter of policy, to deny exemption under the treaty whenever the slightest pretext can be found.
These same experts who made a searching study of the case also declare that the case demonstrates that the United States taxing authorities have adopted a policy of denying exemption to most types of selling commissions, imposing great penalties upon Canadian companies and denying deductions to them and subjecting individual United States investors to personal taxes for the income of Canadian companies which have participated in Canadian developments.
I need not point out to the Minister of Finance that if this policy is pursued by the United States authorities it will have an inevitable and very bad effect upon United States investors in the future, and unless it is changed it will result in very great damage to Canadian development and certainly will be injurious to the financial position of Canada and the provincial governments. It seems quite clear that the policy that they have launched in the United States in this regard can be changed only by firm and direct action on the highest level and then only if the officials of our Department of External Affairs and perhaps of the treasury as well insist that the intent and purpose of the tax treaty must be fully observed and implemented by both governments. Therefore we should not go dawdling along tied to the apron strings of any group in the United States in this regard. We have to stand on our two feet and tell them where to get off when we feel they are not treating the tax treaty as it should be treated.
It ought to be abundantly clear to the government that if they dilly-dally around, if no formal and strong protest against what is happening across the line is made and if as a result Premium's case is lost in the tax court on the ground that there might have been a slight activity in the United States by what has been declared a "permanent establishment", then the results will be very far-reaching. The rule of that case will undoubtedly be applied to collect United States taxes for past as well as future years from a good many Canadian corporations that, up to this time, have been thought to be exempt from United States taxation.
There is a feature about the case, which seems to me pretty fantastic. It is that the

United States tax assessments against Premium Iron Ores are on the basis of gross and not net income. That is almost unheard of. The taxing authorities down there seem to take the position that a Canadian company is subject to heavy penalties and is not entitled to deduct taxes paid to Canada and the provinces or other expenses where the company has failed to file United States tax returns on time even though, as in Premium's case, the company and the Canadian government had good reason to believe that no United States tax returns were required to be filed. This again illustrates how primitive the attitude of the United States tax authorities can be, and my judgment tells me that it indicates considerable hostility towards the treaty exemptions and Canadian companies which, in good faith, avail themselves of these exemptions.
Many thousands of Canadian people from one coast to the other are disturbed about this whole situation. They believe that when the United States attempts to assess taxation against United States investors in a Canadian development company it strikes right at the root of something pretty fundamental, and unless it is carefully handled at the policy level-no other level is capable of handling it-the economy of Canada and the economies of the different provinces of this country are likely to get a pretty severe jolt.
I raise the question only because I am concerned about a very large number of companies which have been financed in exactly the same way as Premium. This company's case certainly is not unique in any sense of the word and United States investors in this company have in this instance financed in exactly the same way as United States investors have in many other instances in Canada, some of which affect my own province. But if what the United States is now trying to do is allowed to become law without any protest from Canada, then no company of the kind would be safe. I suggest that Canada must move before it does become law in the United States. We should not be sitting idly by while an attempt is being made to rewrite unilaterally the whole United States-Canada tax treaty.
I might point out for the benefit of my hon. friends, the Minister of Finance and the Minister of National Revenue that in the United States they have a law which provides that 25 per cent of any tax that is collected may be paid to informers who inform the department of internal revenue of that country that someone is liable to pay tax. In this case that in itself becomes a dangerous thing because involved are more than $4
The Budget-Mr. Low
million in back taxes, and 25 per cent of that amount is $1 million. One million dollars is a lot of money with which to tempt some people into getting information.
I certainly suggest-and this is the reason I asked the minister the question which I did the other day-that we have to watch these things most carefully especially when there is a pernicious law like that on the statute books of the United States. As I said, a million dollars can buy a lot of information. Information has been bought around here in the past week or ten days without a million dollars about which the minister knows something. I would strongly urge that we watch this situation most carefully.
I should like to turn now for a few minutes to something a little more pleasant. I think I can make a suggestion whereby the Minister of Finance can save some money. I think the government should welcome our efforts any time we can find a way to save some money. It has occurred to me for a long time now that our nationally owned broadcasting system could be operated on a far more efficient and economic basis if instead of maintaining what is a costly coast to coast network of C.B.C. stations for more than 18 hours a day, seven days a week, as is now the case, the C.B.C. would prepare a few high quality programs each day and have them released by the privately-owned stations on a contractual basis. I should think that this would save the expenditure of millions of dollars every year, and yet I believe it would provide far better coverage for C.B.C. programs than they get now because I think the minister realizes that a good many more people listen to the privately-owned stations than listen to the C.B.C. That is the record.
I am not saying that in any critical sense at all but simply stating it as a fact.
I think everybody realizes that broadcasting conditions have changed in the past few years. The outstanding network programs of former days do not exist any more. I am referring, for instance, to programs such as the ones on which Jack Benny, Bob Hope and Eddie Cantor appeared, all these great entertainers who used to be commercially sponsored and were used to make the radio network profitable. But they are on television now and radio has gone what is called "local", with the exception of news and special events which I consider to be good programs.
I see no earthly use at all of the C.B.C. owning and operating stations from coast to coast for the purpose of broadcasting gramophone records which already are being broadcast by the privately-owned stations. The financial butter is being spread altogether too thinly now, and that has been one of the

The Budget-Mr. Low
main complaints both by the C.B.C. and by the people who listen to the C.B.C. throughout the whole country. It is costing the treasury more and more every year, with increasing television expenses to be added to the cost of radio.
Take a look at station CBO in Ottawa.
I have nothing against the station but it is a fair sample of what one finds all over the country. If the information I have obtained is correct, and I think it is, that C.B.C. station employs a staff of about 75 people. It contributes three 15-minute programs a week to the network. In the city of Regina, according to my information, the C.B.C. employs 54 people who do not produce a single program for the network.
This is unproductive work which could just as easily be done by the private stations and which is duplicated a good many times over throughout Canada.
If the C.B.C. would produce a few national broadcasts a day, perhaps special features for farming, fishing and labour, and a few good musical and dramatic programs, in my judgment it would be doing a fine job. These programs could be carried by the private stations which are covering Canada already without the necessity of the C.B.C. network. C.B.C. features would be better then because they would be concentrating their efforts and money into a few hours a day instead of trying to provide an 18-hour service over five different time zones throughout Canada.
With some of the millions of dollars that could be saved through this system of operation the C.B.C. could make a real effort to encourage the development of music and dramatic talent across this country. One of the great difficulties of developing first-rate talent today is the lack of enough teachers and producers available for local groups. The C.B.C. could have a talent development section that would supply local groups with music and scripts which they could work on themselves; and then at the proper time the services of a C.B.C. producer might be provided in order to bring them along to broadcast standard when they are ready.
I think this suggestion is well worth the careful consideration of the government and the C.B.C. May I say, Mr. Speaker, that I have not written to the C.B.C. about it, but I imagine I could do so perhaps without being accused of attempting to interfere with C.B.C. programming.

subtopic: ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Since the Minister of Finance presented his annual statement, more commonly known as his annual budget, I have followed with great interest the speeches made in the house by hon. members from both sides and from all parties. In the eight days allotted to this debate the members of all parties have expressed their own opinions. As one might expect, some were favourable while others were most critical and could see this budget as nothing but an unrealistic document which offered nothing but unimportant concessions. For my part, I want to congratulate the Minister of Finance (Mr. Harris) on his expressed moderate optimism, for his lack of exaggeration and his sound comprehension of our Canadian economy. His significant budgetary surplus is most justifiable and desirable at a time when there is every indication that the demand for goods and services is creating a trend towards possible inflation, and at a time when every possible measure should be taken to help combat inflationary pressures in our Canadian economy.
The budget presented in this house on March 14 last was a tax setting document which, in greater or lesser degree, had something for just about every Canadian citizen. The members of the opposition parties are not serious when they are criticizing the government for failing to produce any major changes in the tax structure, and particularly in the income tax field. The Canadian public, fully conscious of our inflationary pressures, were not expecting concessions or deductions

of major consequence. However, every thinking citizen of this country will recognize this budget as one of cheer to Canadians of all ages in which levies were reduced by $128 million. It was a budget designed to increase further the humanitarian measures intended to assure for Canadians a social standard comparable to that of any other people throughout the world. This aim is well proven by increased disbursements to all classes amounting to $133 million.
The amendments moved by both the conservatives and C.C.F. were well identified by their demands for increased old age pensions, as well as deductions in income tax. These matters have been dealt with in detail by members from the government side who have preceded me in this debate. The parliamentary assistant to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Benidickson) has mentioned the increased estimates of Conservative governments in Ontario and New Brunswick, where spendings were forecast at all time highs. Since then the estimates have been tabled in Nova Scotia, where there is another Conservative government, and here again expenditures will be increased by approximately $6,800,000, an all time record.
The Tory members from New Brunswick have been brisk in complimenting our present New Brunswick government for its achievements, and in the same breath criticizing the federal government for its lack of generosity towards the Canadian people. I realize that $6 per month for old age pensioners, for invalids and for blind and disabled persons, may not seem satisfactory to the recipients of those pensions, but at the same time it will mean an additional outlay of $66 million per year to these classes of people whose income is limited and in most cases more or less stabilized. These same people have not forgotten that it was a Liberal government which introduced these security measures, originally on a basis of $20 monthly, and that it was a Liberal government which has provided gradual increases until today the rate of $46 per month has been proposed.
The increase of $42 million a year in family allowances may not seem much to opposition members, but to us on the government side it means much more than the refusal of the Conservative convention held in Ottawa on December 13 last to even consider recommending an increase in the rate at which these allowances are presently being paid.
The increase of $25 million in payments under the Pension Act and the War Veterans Allowance Act may not seem generous enough to opposition members, but even this increase

may not have been possible had their excessive demands in other security fields been met.
The opposition critics have not recognized the importance of one of the more notable adjustments in the budget which was made with the hope of increasing savings and thereby curbing inflation. This provision which allows income tax deductions to individuals purchasing certain annuities will, aside from encouraging Canadians to save, provide the self-employed people with a retirement security fund deductible from yearly taxable income.
The 1957 budget, Mr. Speaker, is much more generous than the one presented a day earlier in the New Brunswick legislature. There we had clear evidence of increased expenditure with the only reduction being the abolition of a three per cent sales tax on dynamite-
