The 1957 budget is a wise and generous one. It has been accepted, not only as a family budget but also as a far-reaching new deal designed to breathe new life into the economy and offer a long-range development program to the Atlantic provinces. The announcement of proposed new and immediate assistance toward the alleviation of the freight rates and power problems in the Atlantic provinces is a clear indication of the intention of the present government to co-operate in the great task of developing the rich natural resources of our country. The federal government has been requesting for years a sound and economical proposal or scheme from the Atlantic provinces that could be implemented on its merits. I will admit that opposition members from New Brunswick, and I could add from the Atlantic provinces, have been eager to criticize this government at every opportunity. We have heard such expressions as traitor, saboteurs; we have heard cries for justice and the government has been accused of being disloyal, of refusing to endorse a note for the construction of Beechwood.
The Budget-Mr. Robichaud
During all this time the present government was taking a realistic view of the situation, and at the same time was taking a positive and comprehensive approach to the problems facing the Atlantic provinces. The government has studied seriously certain recommendations contained in the Gordon report and already, within less than three months from the presentation of this report, is prepared to implement some of its most important recommendations.
The announcement of a plan for federal construction of thermal power plants and of interconnecting lines between the provinces of New Brunswick and Nova Scotia is regarded as a most encouraging development. The development of this system, together with further implementation of this program by the government now and by this government after June next, will assure full development and processing of mineral resources in New Brunswick, and more particularly in the northern sections of the province.
Already representatives of both provinces have met with officials of the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources and judging from press releases, have arrived at a most satisfactory mutual understanding. In my constituency of Gloucester, where major deposits of lead, zinc and copper are presently under development, this announcement of a reasonably low cost supply of power has been received with great satisfaction. We can provide at Bathurst in proximity to the mining deposits port facilities to handle by water the transportation of coal from the mining centres of Cape Breton and other sections of Nova Scotia. We have in Pokesudie, at a distance of only 60 miles from the mining areas, port facilities which could handle year round, without interruption, any amount of coal which could be required to generate the necessary power for the mining of our minerals.

speechtext:
This most important decision of the federal government could well mean the assurance of a smelter for northern New Brunswick and the processing within our border of the base metals produced in the area. We can now regard as a reality the supply of additional electric power which was always regarded as a key to the maximum development of New Brunswick's mineral deposits.
I am convinced that the so-called "nebulous proposal affecting the maritime provinces" as expressed in this house on March 22 by the hon. member for Saint John-Albert (Mr. Bell) could well prove to be the most important decision and the most logical answer to the problems of the Atlantic provinces. When the hon. member is given a chance- and it may be sooner than he expects-to consider the effect of this decision in his own city of Saint John he may change his mind completely and be most embarrassed to explain his attitude to the electors of his constituency. The only nebulous part of the deal could well be the words or expression used by the hon. member on that occasion.
On Monday, March 18, the leader of the official opposition addressed a Conservative convention in Fredericton, the capital city of my own province. On that occasion he accused the Liberal members from New Brunswick of being rubber stamps and yes-men for the right hon. Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe). I am not ashamed to be a yes-man for the Minister of Trade and Commerce, whose reputation is well-known as one of the greatest Canadians who ever lived. His contributions to his country in wartime and in peacetime will long be remembered and his name will be highly regarded in Canadian history. I would rather be a yes-man to the minister who has sponsored such great projects as we have witnessed in this country in the last 20 years, and would rather support such bills as the Trans-Canada Pipe Lines bill, than to have any connection with a party or parties which have so earnestly and vigorously opposed measures designed for the development of our natural resources.

On the same occasion the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) is reported as saying that the member for Restigouche-Madawaska had "dehorned" the Liberal members from New Brunswick. If this statement can be considered as an approval of the hon. member's tactics, as an approval of his statements and expressions used in this house, if this can be considered as an approval of his accusations against the Minister of Labour (Mr. Gregg), I want him to know now that his approval was given in the wrong place and at the wrong time. The people of York-Sunbury will not stand for anyone calling, or approving the calling of, the Minister of Labour a saboteur.
If that is the policy to be adopted by the Conservative party in the coming election they may as well make up their minds right now that this is a land of peace-loving people tied together by bonds of unity and respect and that such attitudes will get them nowhere.
In the course of his remarks on Saturday, March 30, the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Van Horne) referred to a Liberal nominating convention held in his constituency on Sunday, March 17. He considered it an insult to people of many faiths in his riding to hold a convention on Sunday afternoon while church services were being held. We all know that on Sundays church services are normally held in the morning or in the evening.
I hold in my hand a true copy of an announcement which was made over station CJEM, Edmundston, on Friday, March 15. It reads as follows, and I translate:
The member Van Horne is detained at United Nations in New York and he will not be in Edmundston Saturday, but he will be present at the big meeting Sunday, and will be at the disposal of all Sunday night at the office on Canada street.
It is a crime, an insult for the Liberals to hold a convention on Sunday afternoon, but it is permissible for the hon. member to have his meeting on Sunday evening at an hour when church services are normally being held.
No one at that meeting ever said that the hon. member was not in New York on the day previous, but we made it clear that he had no business to be detained at the United Nations at that time. By using his own words I could say: How ridiculous can he be? How far can he stretch the truth? It is not right that he should do that. How far can he stretch the truth when right here in this house he himself shifted back from Saturday to Friday and then to Thursday in order to try and make us believe there was a special meeting of

the committee on resolutions of the United Nations being held on those days. We know now of the special interest he had toward his friends the Cameroons. Who is playing on the ignorance of people?
We all know of the hon. member's remarks at the Spadina Tory convention in Toronto a few weeks ago, where he declared that in his own riding, at his own by-election, the Liberals were giving away money and television sets to buy votes. In this house on Saturday last he stretched the truth and his imagination by saying that such incidents took place in the neighbouring riding of Temiscouata. In a few days he will likely stretch his imagination still further and maybe move into my own constituency of Gloucester. I hope he has not forgotten his series of oyster parties and orgies which he himself had during his 1955 by-election campaign. His charge that during the campaign I said, "If you vote for Van Horne you will lose your old age pensions and family allowances" is absolutely false, and there again he is stretching his imagination and distorting the facts, as he has done so often in this house and outside.
His charges of Tobacco Road look in northern New Brunswick is another example of his imagination and dim approach to any situation. We do admit that we have in northern New Brunswick certain areas where people are badly in need of assistance, but such conditions are not typical of our province alone. These problems need a more comprehensive and realistic approach than irresponsible charges and accusations such as we have heard from the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska.
The hon. member was quick to notice my absence from my seat when he spoke on Saturday last. I shall not mention his attendance record for fear that he may again seek the excuse of attending the United Nations special committee on resolutions. If I left Ottawa on Saturday afternoon it was to go to my own constituency and discuss with certain authorities the possibility of a large low rental housing project for aged people under the Central Mortgage and Housing program.
